guides.title: Footpath dining permit (Cairns Regional Council)
guides.summary: To put tables, chairs, umbrellas, planter boxes or barriers on the Council footpath outside your cafe or restaurant in Cairns you need a footpath dining permit (a Commercial Use Activity permit under Council's local laws). You pay a one-off application fee for a 1, 2 or 3 year permit plus a rental fee per square metre that depends on the area of the city, and you must hold A$20 million public liability insurance.
guides.authority: Cairns Regional Council, under Local Law No. 11 (Local Government Controlled Areas and Roads) 2016 and Local Law No. 1 (Administration) 2016
guides.timeframe: Minimum 14 days and up to 30 days. Council will not accept an application with a start date less than 14 days after you submit it.
guides.cost_summary: 2026-27 application fee A$290 (1 year), A$525 (2 years) or A$750 (3 years), plus rental per square metre from A$11.90 (Area G) to A$247.20 (Area A).
before_you_start: Read Council's Best Practice Use of Footpaths Policy; applications are assessed against it, including pedestrian clearances and furniture standards.
If you do not own or hold a registered lease over the adjoining premises, get the landowner's written consent.
Get a certificate of currency for public liability insurance of at least A$20 million in the permit holder's name, noting Cairns Regional Council as an interested party.
If the area is next to a state-controlled road you also need a Department of Transport and Main Roads approval.
If alcohol will be served in the area, your liquor licence must cover it; give Council the licence at least 7 days before the permit starts.
Your food business licence assessment considers whether you hold the footpath dining permit you need, so apply early.

steps.title: Measure the area and prepare a site plan
steps.detail: Draw a site plan showing the permit area dimensions, adjoining buildings, footpath and kerb, furniture and structures, and nearby permanent infrastructure (poles, bins, trees). Council has a sample site plan on its footpath dining page.

steps.title: Gather attachments
steps.detail: Attach colour photos of the area, photos or brochures of furniture and structures, a written procedure covering amenity, nuisance to neighbours and pedestrian thoroughfare, landowner consent if needed, other approvals (TMR, liquor licence), and the A$20 million public liability certificate of currency.

steps.title: Lodge the application
steps.detail: Apply online (Commercial Use Activity footpath dining permit) or submit the PDF form by email to regadmin@cairns.qld.gov.au, by mail, or in person at the Spence Street customer service centre. Choose a 1, 2 or 3 year term. Council sends payment instructions once it has a complete application.
steps.timeframe: Lodge at least 14 days, ideally 30 days, before the start date
steps.cost: A$290, A$525 or A$750 depending on term

form.name: Commercial Use Activity: footpath dining permit application (2026/2027)

steps.title: Pay rental and set up to the conditions
steps.detail: Pay the rental for your area (charged per square metre by area category A to G; not charged where you already pay rent under a road permit). Keep the insurance current for the whole permit and keep furniture within the approved area.
steps.cost: A$11.90 to A$247.20 per square metre

fees.note: Rent then charged under the road permit

Menu stands and sandwich board signs are prohibited in the Cairns CBD.
No alcohol may be consumed in the area until you have the liquor licence covering it.

guides.title: Workers' compensation accident insurance policy (WorkCover Queensland)
guides.summary: If your Queensland business employs workers, including casuals, apprentices and unpaid interns, you must insure them with a WorkCover Queensland accident insurance policy (unless you are a self-insurer). It takes 5 to 15 minutes to apply online. Being uninsured can cost you the unpaid premium plus a 100% penalty, and the cost of any claim plus 50%.
guides.authority: WorkCover Queensland (insurer); Workers' Compensation Regulatory Services, Office of Industrial Relations (regulator)
guides.timeframe: Apply online in about 5 to 15 minutes; you give your workers' start date when you apply. Renew every year between 1 July and 30 September.
guides.cost_summary: Premium = (estimated wages / 100) x your industry rate, plus GST and stamp duty. The 2026-27 average rate across Queensland is A$1.343 per A$100 of wages; your industry rate may be higher or lower. 3% discount for early payment.
before_you_start: You need a policy if you employ workers. A worker is generally a PAYG employee. Some contractors with ABNs are still workers in law; use WorkCover's worker determination tests or the ATO tools if you are unsure.
Apprentices are workers. Unpaid interns have been workers since 1 July 2020 (volunteers, school work experience and registered vocational placements are not).
Directors, partners, sole traders and trustees are not covered by the accident policy. Consider WorkCover's Workplace Personal Injury Insurance for yourself.

Have ready: your workers' start date, estimated wages from today to 30 June (before tax and super), a short description of your main business activity (sets your WorkCover Industry Classification), ABN and ACN, GST status, trading name and physical address, and trustee details if you pay through a trust.
Wages count before tax, superannuation and other deductions.

steps.title: Apply for an accident insurance policy
steps.detail: Apply online through WorkCover's new business system or by phone on 1300 927 928. Any authorised person, such as a director or finance officer, can apply. Give your expected start date, estimated wages, business activity and ABN.

form.name: WorkCover online application for accident insurance policy

steps.title: Check your industry classification and rate
steps.detail: Your WorkCover Industry Classification (WIC) sets your industry rate, which is published each year in the Queensland Government Gazette. Make sure the description of your main activity is accurate, as the wrong WIC means the wrong premium.

steps.title: Pay the first premium
steps.detail: For a business under 18 months old the premium is (estimated wages / 100) x industry rate, plus GST and stamp duty. Pay online through WorkCover Connect, BPAY (biller code 182006), card (1300 132 278), direct debit or cheque. Interest-free payment plans are available for premiums over A$200.
steps.cost: Wages / 100 x industry rate, plus GST and stamp duty

steps.title: Renew and declare wages every year
steps.detail: Each July WorkCover contacts you. Declare actual wages for the year just ended and estimates for the new year, then pay between 1 July and 30 September. Declare by 31 August and pay in full by 16 September for a 3% discount; declaring by 31 August is also needed to set up a payment plan.

steps.title: Keep your policy accurate
steps.detail: Update WorkCover when your business activity, wages or structure changes. After 18 months your rate depends on your claims history (policy rating 80% to 120% of the industry rate), and businesses with wages over A$1.5 million move to experience-based rating.

fees.label: Average premium rate 2026-27 (statewide)
fees.note: Unchanged from 2025-26; your rate depends on your industry

fees.label: Early payment discount
fees.note: Declare wages by 31 August and pay in full by 16 September

fees.label: Penalty for unpaid or under-declared premium
fees.note: On top of the unpaid premium

fees.note: WorkCover can recover compensation or damages it paid plus 50%

contacts.note: Email is for direct debit or deposit confirmations

watch_out: 1300 362 128 is the Office of Industrial Relations (WorkSafe). For your policy, quotes and payments call WorkCover Queensland on 1300 927 928.
If you do not pay by 30 September your cover ends. A worker injured while your premium is unpaid can leave you liable for the claim cost.
WorkCover audits employers. Under-declared wages attract the unpaid premium plus a penalty equal to 100% of it, and matters can be referred for prosecution.
Calling a worker a contractor does not avoid the obligation; having an ABN does not settle whether someone is a worker.
Your own injuries as a sole trader, partner or director are not covered by the accident policy.
Workers interstate or overseas may need cover in another state; check with WorkCover.

guides.title: Register for PAYG withholding and set up as an employer
guides.summary: Before you pay your first employee you must register for pay as you go (PAYG) withholding with the ATO, even if no tax ends up being withheld. Taking on staff also brings other duties: Single Touch Payroll reporting, super paid with every pay (Payday Super from 1 July 2026, 12% of qualifying earnings), TFN declarations, Fair Work information statements and award pay rates.
guides.authority: Australian Taxation Office (ATO); Fair Work Ombudsman for pay and conditions
guides.timeframe: Register before your first payment that you need to withhold from. Super must reach the fund within 7 business days of each payday.
guides.cost_summary: The ATO lists no fee to register. Your ongoing costs are wages, 12% super, workers compensation insurance (state based) and STP-enabled payroll software.
before_you_start: Decide whether the worker is an employee or an independent contractor; the obligations are very different. Contractors who do not quote an ABN also trigger withholding.
Check the worker has the right to work in Australia. If you hire a working holiday maker, register as an employer of working holiday makers before you pay them.
Set up access to ATO Online services for business: get a Digital ID such as myID, then link it to your business in Relationship Authorisation Manager (RAM).
Get payroll software that is Single Touch Payroll (STP) enabled.

Find the award that covers the job (most small businesses are covered by one) and the minimum pay rate. The national minimum wage from the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026 is A$26.44 an hour or A$1,005 a week for employees not covered by an award.
Choose a default super fund and a SuperStream-compliant way to pay. The Small Business Superannuation Clearing House closed permanently on 1 July 2026.
Arrange workers compensation insurance in your state or territory and work out whether payroll tax or fringe benefits tax applies to you.

Even if you do not have an ABN (for example you employ a nanny, cleaner, cook or gardener privately, or self-manage NDIS funds and employ staff), you still need to register for a PAYG withholding account.

steps.title: Register for PAYG withholding
steps.detail: With an ABN: register through the Business Registration Service, Online services for business, your registered tax or BAS agent, SBR-enabled software, or by phoning the ATO business line as an authorised contact. Without an ABN: phone the business line or lodge the Application to register a PAYG withholding account (NAT 3377). You must register before the first payment you need to withhold from, even if the amount withheld is nil.

form.name: Application to register a PAYG withholding account (NAT 3377)

steps.title: Give the employee their information statements
steps.detail: Give every new employee the Fair Work Information Statement before, or as soon as possible after, they start. Casual employees must also get the Casual Employment Information Statement, and employees on a fixed term contract must also get the Fixed Term Contract Information Statement. Make their award easily available to them.
steps.timeframe: Before or as soon as possible after the first day

steps.title: Collect the TFN declaration
steps.detail: Ask the employee to complete a Tax file number declaration (online through their ATO online services commencement forms, which they must complete within 28 days of starting, or on paper). If you use STP-enabled software you keep the form and do not send it to the ATO. If you are not using STP and get a paper form, complete section B and send it to the ATO within 14 days. If no TFN is provided and no exemption applies, withhold at the top rate plus Medicare levy (after 28 days if they have applied for a TFN).

steps.title: Offer choice of super fund
steps.detail: Give the employee a Superannuation standard choice form. If they do not choose a fund, you may need to ask the ATO for their stapled super fund before using your default fund. Give their TFN to the fund the next time you contribute or within 14 days of receiving it, whichever is later.

steps.title: Pay correctly and give a payslip
steps.detail: Pay at least the award or national minimum rate, withhold tax using the ATO tax tables, set the withheld tax aside, and give a payslip within one working day of payday. Use the Fair Work Pay Calculator to check rates, penalties and allowances.
steps.timeframe: Payslip within 1 working day of payday

steps.title: Report every pay through Single Touch Payroll
steps.detail: Report each employee's pay, tax withheld and super to the ATO through STP every time you pay them. Make an end-of-year finalisation declaration through STP by 14 July each year.

steps.title: Pay super with every pay (Payday Super)
steps.detail: From 1 July 2026 you must pay super guarantee of 12% of qualifying earnings (ordinary time earnings, paid leave, allowances, bonuses, commissions and superable salary sacrifice) so it is received by the employee's fund within 7 business days after each payday. For a new employee, or an employee who has moved to a new fund, the first contribution has 20 business days. Pay through a SuperStream-compliant method.
steps.timeframe: Received by the fund within 7 business days of payday

steps.title: Report and pay withheld tax on your BAS
steps.detail: Include PAYG withholding amounts on your business activity statement and pay the ATO the amounts you withheld.

steps.title: Keep records
steps.detail: Keep employment records for 7 years and tax and super records for 5 years, stored safely. When employment ends, give final pay (including unused annual leave) within 7 days.

fees.label: Super guarantee rate
fees.note: Rate from 1 July 2025 onwards (Norfolk Island 11% from 1 July 2026). Not a fee, a minimum contribution.

fees.label: National minimum wage
fees.note: From the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026; award rates may be higher

fees.label: Super maximum contribution base 2026-27
fees.note: Above this level of qualifying earnings in a year, minimum super is no longer required for that employee

contacts.name: ATO business enquiries
contacts.hours: 8:00 am to 6:00 pm Monday to Friday

contacts.name: Fair Work Infoline
contacts.hours: 8am to 5:30pm Monday to Friday
contacts.note: Pay rates, awards and employment conditions

watch_out: Super that reaches the fund after the 7 business day deadline is late and can attract the super guarantee charge, even if you pay it later. A rejected payment does not extend the deadline.
The Small Business Superannuation Clearing House closed on 1 July 2026; do not rely on it.
Calling an employee a contractor, or asking them to get an ABN, does not change their legal status and can leave you owing tax, super and entitlements.
Underpaying award rates is a common and costly mistake. Check the award and the Pay Calculator before the first pay.
You must give the Fair Work Information Statement to every new employee, plus the casual or fixed term statement where it applies.
Workers compensation insurance and payroll tax are state or territory obligations and are not covered by the ATO registration.

guides.title: Register with AICIS before you import or manufacture industrial chemicals
guides.summary: If you import or manufacture industrial chemicals for commercial purposes in Australia, including products that contain them such as cosmetics, cleaning products, paints and inks, your business must be registered with the Australian Industrial Chemicals Introduction Scheme (AICIS) before you introduce them. Registration runs for a registration year from 1 September to 31 August, and introducing chemicals while unregistered is an offence under the Industrial Chemicals Act 2019.
guides.authority: Australian Industrial Chemicals Introduction Scheme (AICIS)
guides.timeframe: Register online before your first introduction; the 2026-27 registration year runs 1 September 2026 to 31 August 2027, and you renew each year before 1 September. Annual declarations are due by 30 November after each registration year ends.
guides.cost_summary: For 2026-27 (from 1 September 2026) you pay an A$85 registration fee plus a levy based on the value of chemicals you introduced in the previous financial year. Because of a one-off 90% levy discount, totals range from A$85 (level 1, under A$50,000) to A$3,585 (level 8, A$15 million or more). No GST applies.
before_you_start: Work out whether you are an introducer: AICIS says anyone who imports or manufactures industrial chemicals for commercial purposes must register, including businesses, sole traders and individuals, and including people importing products that contain industrial chemicals.

Add up the value of the industrial chemicals you imported or manufactured in the previous financial year (for 2026-27 registration, 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026). This sets your registration level. If you are registering for the first time and introduced nothing in that period, you are level 1.
Have your business details ready so you can enrol in AICIS Business Services, the online portal used for registration, renewals and declarations.

Be ready to categorise every chemical you introduce. Each chemical (including each ingredient in a mixture) must fall into one of five categories: listed, exempted, reported, assessed, or commercial evaluation authorisation. AICIS publishes free decision tools to help.

Set up a record-keeping system from day one. AICIS says you must keep records for 5 years, even after you stop introducing the chemical, and provide them within 20 working days if asked (stated for assessed introductions).
If you will not introduce industrial chemicals after 31 August, tell AICIS through the 'advise of non-renewal' option in AICIS Business Services rather than just letting registration lapse.

steps.title: Work out your registration level
steps.detail: Use the AICIS registration calculator. Your level is based on the total value of industrial chemicals you imported or manufactured in the previous financial year (1 July to 30 June). The calculator also shows your fee and levy. Level 1 is A$0 to A$49,999 and level 8 is A$15,000,000 or more.

steps.title: Enrol in AICIS Business Services
steps.detail: New users create an account in AICIS Business Services, the AICIS online portal. Follow the AICIS guidance on creating an account. Renewing users simply log in. AICIS has tips on usernames and resetting passwords if you are locked out.

steps.title: Register or renew for the registration year
steps.detail: In AICIS Business Services, open the Registration section and select the registration year (2026-27). Enter your registration level and pay the registration fee and levy. You must be registered before you introduce industrial chemicals on or after 1 September 2026.
steps.timeframe: Before your first introduction in the registration year (registration year starts 1 September)
steps.cost: A$85 to A$3,585 for 2026-27 depending on level

steps.title: Categorise each chemical before you introduce it
steps.detail: For every chemical, decide its category. Listed: already on the Australian Inventory of Industrial Chemicals; meet any listing terms. Exempted: very low risk; no pre-notification, but some need a once-off post-introduction declaration. Reported: low risk; submit a once-off pre-introduction report before you start. Assessed: medium to high risk; you need an assessment certificate (fee applies) before you import or manufacture. Commercial evaluation authorisation: time-limited, for testing commercial viability (fee applies).
steps.timeframe: Before introduction (reported and assessed categories need action before you import)
steps.cost: No fee for listed, exempted or reported; fees apply for assessment certificates and commercial evaluation authorisations

steps.title: Keep records for every introduction
steps.detail: Keep records showing how you categorised each chemical and that you met the category requirements. AICIS says its decision tools are general guidance only and a completed decision tool is not enough on its own to meet your record-keeping obligations. Keep records for 5 years.

steps.title: Lodge your annual declaration
steps.detail: After each registration year, declare in AICIS Business Services that the chemicals you introduced were authorised. Submissions open in August. If you introduced nothing, select 'Did not introduce' in the portal. Example from AICIS: introductions between 1 September 2023 and 31 August 2024 had to be declared by 30 November 2024.
steps.timeframe: Due 30 November after the end of each registration year

steps.title: Renew every year, or tell AICIS you are stopping
steps.detail: Renew in AICIS Business Services for the new registration year before you introduce chemicals on or after 1 September. If you are stopping, use 'advise of non-renewal' for the new year.

fees.note: 2026-27, from 1 September 2026. Fee only, no levy.

contacts.name: AICIS
contacts.note: Postal address: GPO Box 58 Sydney NSW 2001. The contact page does not list a general email address.

watch_out: Introducing an industrial chemical without being registered is an offence under the Industrial Chemicals Act 2019. Register before the goods arrive, not after.

Small importers of cosmetics, soaps, cleaning products, fragrances and similar goods often do not realise they are chemical introducers. Importing a product that contains an industrial chemical counts.

The 90% levy discount is one-off for 2026-27 only. From 2027-28 levies return to 2025-26 levels with two years of indexation, so a level 5 business that pays A$295 now could pay over A$2,180 next year.
Your level is based on the previous financial year's introductions, not your expected sales. Under-declaring your level is a compliance risk.
A chemical in the 'assessed' category cannot be imported until you hold an assessment certificate. 'Reported' chemicals need the pre-introduction report lodged before you start.
Missing the 30 November annual declaration is a separate compliance failure, even if you are registered. If you imported nothing, you still select 'Did not introduce'.
Assessment certificate application fees rose from 1 September 2026 and the certificate application structure changes from 1 July 2027 (five types reduced to three).

guides.title: Get therapeutic goods onto the ARTG before you import and sell them
guides.summary: Medicines, vitamins and supplements, and medical devices must generally be entered in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) before you can lawfully supply them in Australia. An Australian sponsor applies to the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), pays application fees and annual charges, and takes legal responsibility for the product. Importing for your own personal use is a separate, limited scheme and cannot be used for resale.
guides.authority: Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA)
guides.timeframe: Medical devices: the TGA makes its preliminary assessment decision within 20 business days of a paid application, longer if selected for audit. Listed (AUST L) medicines are validated electronically and listed on submission; registered medicines take much longer.
guides.cost_summary: From 1 July 2026: a listed medicine (AUST L) costs A$1,063 to apply plus A$1,566 a year; a Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring) medical device costs A$651 to apply plus A$121 a year; Class IIa/IIb devices A$1,244 plus A$1,305 a year; Class III A$1,603 plus A$1,662 a year. Audits and registered medicines cost much more.
before_you_start: Confirm your product is a therapeutic good at all. Some products are regulated as foods or cosmetics instead, and some goods are excluded or exempt (Schedules 5, 5A and 7 of the Therapeutic Goods Regulations 1990 list product exemptions).

Search the ARTG. If the product is already on it, you may be able to buy from the existing sponsor and sell as a retailer instead of becoming a sponsor yourself, though commercial agreements may prevent this.

Decide who will be the sponsor. The sponsor is the person or company that supplies the goods in Australia and is legally responsible for them. If you import directly from the manufacturer and are the first point of supply, you need TGA approval as sponsor.

For medical devices, get a written agreement with your manufacturer so you can obtain technical information quickly. You must answer TGA information requests within set timeframes and allow inspections.

Confirm the manufacturer meets requirements: overseas medicine sites need GMP clearance, and device manufacturers need conformity assessment evidence (for example an overseas certificate the TGA accepts) or a TGA conformity assessment certificate.
For listed (AUST L) supplements, check every ingredient is a permitted ingredient and every claim is a permitted indication, and hold evidence for your claims before you list.
Budget for ongoing annual charges and post-market duties: adverse event reporting, recalls, advertising code compliance, and keeping records (devices: up to 10 years or the device's lifetime).

steps.title: Create a TGA Business Services (TBS) account and register your organisation
steps.detail: Sponsors and manufacturers must register their details with the TGA before seeking approval. TGA Business Services (also called eBS) is the primary application portal for applications and ongoing compliance. Keep your contact details current.

steps.title: Medical devices: classify the device and submit manufacturer evidence
steps.detail: Work out the device class and category. Certain Class I, Class 1 IVD and export-only devices need only a manufacturer's declaration of conformity with the application. All others need manufacturer evidence (such as conformity assessment certificates) submitted in TBS and accepted by the TGA before you draft the inclusion application. One accepted piece of evidence can support multiple applications.

steps.title: Medical devices: apply for ARTG inclusion and pay
steps.detail: Lodge the inclusion application in TBS. You receive an invoice after submission and the TGA does not review the application until it is paid. Application fees are non-refundable. The TGA aims to make a preliminary assessment decision within 20 business days. Outcomes are approved, selected for audit (extra time and audit fees), or refused.
steps.timeframe: Preliminary decision within 20 business days of payment
steps.cost: A$651 (Class I) to A$1,603 (Class III) application fee; audit fees from A$4,926 if selected

steps.title: Listed medicines (most vitamins, minerals, herbal supplements): list through the electronic listing facility
steps.detail: Listed complementary medicines can contain only permitted low-risk ingredients and make permitted indications. You apply through the electronic listing facility in TGA eBusiness Services; the application must pass electronic validation, and you certify that the product meets all legal requirements. The TGA does not evaluate the claims before listing, but runs random and targeted compliance reviews. Each listed product gets an AUST L number that must appear on the label.
steps.timeframe: Listed once the application validates and is submitted
steps.cost: A$1,063 application fee and A$1,566 annual charge (from 1 July 2026)

steps.title: Registered medicines: apply for evaluation
steps.detail: Higher-risk products (registered complementary medicines, over-the-counter medicines and prescription medicines) are evaluated before they are entered on the ARTG. Fees depend on the application level (for example OTC N1 to N5, registered complementary RCM1 to RCM5).

steps.title: Pay annual charges and claim the annual charge exemption if eligible
steps.detail: Annual charges are levied in July each year for every ARTG entry that existed at any time in the financial year. Products entered on or after 1 July 2015 can get an annual charge exemption until they generate turnover. Self-declarations must reach the TGA between 1 July and 22 July each year; late declarations before 15 September cost extra. To avoid next year's charge, ask for cancellation by 30 June.

steps.title: Meet post-market obligations
steps.detail: Report adverse events, support recalls, follow the Therapeutic Goods Advertising Code, keep information on the ARTG current (lodge variations when things change), and for devices notify the TGA within 60 days if manufacturer evidence is suspended, revoked or lapses.

contacts.name: TGA general enquiries
contacts.hours: Monday to Friday, 9 am to 5 pm AEST, excluding public holidays
contacts.note: Post: TGA, PO Box 100, Woden ACT 2606. Written enquiries go through the online enquiry form.

watch_out: Supplying therapeutic goods that are not on the ARTG (and not exempt) can attract civil and criminal penalties.
The Personal Importation Scheme is for you or your immediate family only. Goods imported under it cannot be sold, supplied or given away. It is not a way to test a market.

Personal imports are capped at 3 months' supply per import and 15 months' supply in any 12 months. Prescription-only medicines need a valid Australian prescription at the time of import (eScripts are not accepted).

Vaping products, controlled substances and counterfeit medicines or devices cannot be imported under the Personal Importation Scheme. Some herbal or dietary supplements contain controlled ingredients such as ephedra or DHEA that need a permit.
Non-compliant imports can be seized and destroyed with no compensation, and fines or legal proceedings may follow.
Annual charges apply for every financial year an ARTG entry exists, even if you sold nothing, unless you lodge the exemption declaration between 1 and 22 July. Cancel unwanted entries by 30 June.
From 24 July 2026, nicotine pouches cannot lawfully be imported or supplied unless on the ARTG or covered by a statutory exemption pathway.

guides.title: Equipment licence to import pre-charged refrigeration and air conditioning equipment
guides.summary: If you import refrigeration or air conditioning equipment (including vehicles, boats and other goods with air conditioners) that contains or is designed to use a synthetic greenhouse gas or HCFC refrigerant, you generally need an equipment licence (EQPL) under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Act 1989 before you import. The licence costs A$3,000, lasts 2 years, and comes with 6-monthly reporting and a levy on the gas you import.
guides.authority: National Environmental Protection Agency (National EPA). The licence pages now sit on nationalepa.gov.au; some related pages are still on the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) site.
guides.timeframe: The National EPA aims to assess a complete application within 2 weeks; the legal maximum is 60 days. Apply before you import.
guides.cost_summary: A$3,000 non-refundable licence application fee (every 2 years), plus an import levy of A$165 per metric tonne of synthetic greenhouse gas (HCFCs A$3,000 per ozone depleting potential tonne), waived if the total for a reporting period is A$330 or less. You also need membership of an approved product stewardship scheme. No GST.
before_you_start: Check if you need a licence at all. Equipment using carbon dioxide (R744), hydrocarbons or ammonia (R717) does not need an EQPL.
Small-quantity exemption: you do not need a licence if you import up to 25 kilograms of HFC, PFC, SF6 or NF3 equipment in a calendar year (measured by the gas in the equipment).

Personal-use exemption: vehicles or other equipment you have owned for more than 12 months and are importing for your own use may qualify. Email ozone@dcceew.gov.au before you import or pay the fee to check.

Check the equipment is not banned. Importing and manufacturing HCFC and CFC refrigeration and air conditioning equipment is banned, with limited exceptions. Air conditioning equipment with a refrigerant charge of 2.6 kg or less is also subject to restrictions under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Regulations 1995.
The applicant's legal name must match the Australian Business Register and you need an ABN. A trust cannot hold a licence, so apply in the trustee's name.
Join an approved product stewardship scheme before applying. The licence page names Refrigerant Reclaim Australia as the currently approved scheme, and you must attach evidence of membership.
Have certified identification for the person signing the application, and a trust deed or partnership authority document if relevant.

steps.title: Confirm whether your goods need an EQPL
steps.detail: Work out what gas the equipment contains or is designed to use and how many kilograms you will import in the calendar year. If it is a natural refrigerant (CO2, hydrocarbon, ammonia) or you stay at 25 kg or less of HFC/PFC/SF6/NF3 equipment, you do not need a licence. If unsure whether your import is equipment or bulk gas, contact the regulator.

steps.title: Join a product stewardship scheme
steps.detail: Get evidence that you are a member of an approved product stewardship scheme (currently Refrigerant Reclaim Australia). You attach it to your application.
steps.cost: Scheme membership costs not published on the regulator page

steps.title: Lodge the online EQPL application and pay
steps.detail: Complete the online EQPL application form with your legal name, ABN, addresses, contact people and details of the goods. Attach certified ID of the signatory, stewardship scheme evidence and any trust or partnership documents. Pay the A$3,000 fee with the application unless you have a fee waiver (available for HCFC equipment of 25 kg or less used for certain testing, medical, veterinary, defence, industrial safety or public safety purposes).
steps.timeframe: Aim: 2 weeks from a complete application; maximum 60 days

steps.title: Import under the licence
steps.detail: Import only once the licence is in force. The licence lasts 2 years from when it comes into force unless a shorter period is set.

steps.title: Report every 6 months
steps.detail: Report the equipment and gas you imported. For 1 January to 30 June, reports are due 14 July. For 1 July to 31 December, reports are due 14 January. You do not need to report for a period with no imports or exports. Note: the official page says reporting is 6-monthly, not quarterly.

steps.title: Pay the import levy
steps.detail: You are invoiced the Import/Manufacture Levy based on your report. Levy payments are due 29 August (for January to June) and 1 March (for July to December). The levy is waived if the total for a period is A$330 or less.
steps.cost: A$165 per metric tonne of synthetic greenhouse gas

steps.title: Renew before expiry
steps.detail: Apply to renew at least 14 days before your licence expires.

fees.label: Equipment licence (EQPL) application
fees.note: Non-refundable, even if you no longer need the licence. Licence lasts 2 years. No GST.

fees.label: Import levy, synthetic greenhouse gases
fees.note: Per metric tonne of gas imported

fees.label: Import levy, HCFCs
fees.note: Per ozone depleting potential tonne (equivalent to A$165 per metric tonne of HCFC-22)

fees.label: Levy waiver threshold
fees.note: Levy is waived if your total for a reporting period is A$330 or less

contacts.name: National EPA ozone and synthetic greenhouse gas team (general enquiries)
Import Operations Team (exemptions and eligibility)
contacts.note: The licence FAQ tells you to contact this address before importing or paying the fee if you think an exemption applies.

watch_out: Apply early and before importing: the regulator tells importers to lodge before they import, and assessment can take up to the 60-day legal maximum.
Cars, boats, caravans and other goods with air conditioning can need a licence too, because equipment contained in other equipment is covered.
The 25 kg exemption is per calendar year and counts all your HFC, PFC, SF6 and NF3 equipment imports together.
The A$3,000 fee is not refunded if your application is refused or you change your mind.
Approval is not guaranteed, and HCFC and CFC equipment is banned except in limited circumstances.
Reporting is every 6 months (14 July and 14 January). Missing reports or levy payments is a separate compliance failure.

guides.title: Register as a responsible supplier for electrical equipment (EESS)
guides.summary: If you import or make household-type electrical equipment rated 50 V AC or more (or 120 V DC or more) to sell in Australia, you must be registered as a responsible supplier on the national Electrical Equipment Safety System (EESS) platform, register Level 2 and Level 3 equipment, and mark it with the RCM. Selling unregistered or unmarked in-scope equipment can lead to penalties and cancelled registration.
guides.authority: Electrical Safety Office, Office of Industrial Relations (Queensland) administers the EESS national platform for participating state and territory electrical safety regulators
guides.timeframe: Registration completes once payment clears (BPoint card or BPAY). Level 3 equipment also needs a certificate of conformity from a recognised certifier first, which takes longer.
guides.cost_summary: From 1 July 2026: A$239.74 a year to register as a responsible supplier, plus A$89.85 for each Level 2 or Level 3 equipment registration per year (A$449.25 for 5 years). Level 1 registration is free and voluntary. No GST.
before_you_start: Check whether your product is in scope: designed for household, personal or similar use, rated 50 V AC or more, or 120 V DC or more. Equipment rated 49 V AC or less, or 119 V DC or less, is Level 0 (out of scope).

Work out the risk level using the 'EESS In-scope Equipment Definitions and Risk Levels' document. Level 1 is in scope but not in the Level 2 or 3 definitions; Level 2 and Level 3 are listed equipment types. Level 3 is the highest risk.
You must be a legally identifiable Australian or New Zealand entity with an ABN (or NZ IRD number) and a physical address in Australia or New Zealand.
Decide who will be your Authorised Officer. Whoever completes the registration form is treated as the Authorised Officer and makes the legal declaration that the equipment is electrically safe.

Get test reports against the relevant Australian standard. For Level 2 you need a compliance folder; for Level 3 you need a certificate of conformity issued by a recognised external certification scheme (RECS) certifier or Energy Safe Victoria, listed on the national register.
Plan where the compliance folder will be kept. You must record its exact location (at least a street address) and keep it for 5 years after the registration ends.

steps.title: Register as a responsible supplier on the EESS platform
steps.detail: Your Authorised Officer enters your legal entity details, ABN, trading name, physical address and contact details on the EESS platform (which replaced the old registration database from 14 October 2024) and makes the responsible supplier declaration. You get a supplier username (format E followed by four digits). You can set up an Authorised Representative to register equipment for you.

steps.title: Level 3: get a certificate of conformity
steps.detail: Have the equipment certified by a recognised certifier (eight RECS certifiers, or Energy Safe Victoria). The certificate can be held by anyone, often the overseas manufacturer, must list a current relevant safety standard, and must be listed on the national register. Certificates usually run 5 years.
steps.cost: Certifier fees are set by the certifier (not published by the regulator)

steps.title: Level 2: build your compliance folder
steps.detail: Compliance folders are mandatory for Level 2. They must hold test reports and other evidence the equipment meets the full relevant standard. The FAQ says Level 1 and Level 3 suppliers also need evidence of compliance with the full standard.

steps.title: Register each Level 2 and Level 3 item or family
steps.detail: Register each item or family of equipment on the platform, give the Electrical Equipment Declaration, and choose a term of 1, 2 or 5 years. Level 3 registration cannot run past the certificate of conformity expiry date. Level 1 registration is optional and free. Do not register Level 2 or 3 equipment as Level 1.
steps.cost: A$89.85 (1 year), A$179.70 (2 years), A$449.25 (5 years) per item or family

steps.title: Mark the equipment with the RCM
steps.detail: As responsible supplier, you authorise the Regulatory Compliance Mark. For Level 1 you may do so once you have evidence of compliance; for Level 2 and 3, once the equipment is registered. Follow AS/NZS 4417.1 (and 4417.2 for Level 3), which registered suppliers can download from the platform's Documents tab. You must not sell unmarked in-scope equipment.

steps.title: Renew every year and keep details current
steps.detail: Responsible supplier registration is renewed annually. Keep your details accurate; false or misleading information can lead to penalties including cancellation.

fees.label: Responsible supplier registration
fees.note: Per year, from 1 July 2026. No GST.

fees.label: Level 2 or Level 3 equipment registration, 1 year
Level 2 or Level 3 equipment registration, 2 years
fees.note: eess.gov.au figure; the WorkSafe Queensland page shows A$179.69

fees.label: Level 2 or Level 3 equipment registration, 5 years
fees.note: eess.gov.au figure; the WorkSafe Queensland page shows A$449.23. Level 3 term cannot exceed the certificate's expiry.

contacts.name: EESS Administration, Electrical Safety Office (Queensland)
contacts.note: Email is preferred; include your phone number if you want a call back. Post: EESS Administration, c/o Electrical Safety Office, Office of Industrial Relations, PO Box 820, Lutwyche QLD 4030.

contacts.name: WorkSafe Queensland
contacts.note: General Office of Industrial Relations line

contacts.name: Australian Communications and Media Authority (for radio and EMC requirements that also use the RCM)

watch_out: Selling Level 2 or Level 3 equipment that is not registered carries penalties.
Registering Level 2 or 3 equipment as Level 1 is not permitted and could result in penalties.
You must not sell in-scope equipment without the RCM.
The responsible supplier must be a legally identifiable Australian or New Zealand entity with an ABN or NZ IRD number, so an overseas manufacturer cannot register in your place.
Giving inaccurate details or false or misleading information can lead to penalties, including cancellation of your registration.
Level 3 registration ends when the certificate of conformity expires, even if you paid for a longer term.
Plugs, cords and cord sets sold as an integral part of other equipment do not need separate registration if a valid certificate of conformity for them is listed on the national register.

guides.title: Permission to import firearms, weapons, parts and ammunition
guides.summary: Firearms, firearm parts and accessories, ammunition, imitation firearms and many weapons (such as daggers, crossbows and throwing knives) are prohibited imports unless you meet an import test and hold the right police certification or Home Affairs permission before they arrive. Rules were tightened from 22 January 2026: ongoing police certifications were cancelled, and more items now need a Home Affairs permit.
guides.authority: Department of Home Affairs and Australian Border Force (ABF), with state and territory police firearms and weapons registries for police certification
guides.timeframe: Allow about four weeks for an ABF permission application (form B710) once all information is received. Police certification times vary by state.
guides.cost_summary: The ABF B710 form does not list an application fee. State and territory police may charge for B709 certification and licences; check with your registry.
before_you_start: You must hold the right state or territory licence, permit to acquire or other authority to possess the item where you live. In Queensland, for example, a permit to acquire is needed for any weapon that must be registered to a licence, and ammunition imports still need a B709 even though your licence gives import authority.

Identify which control applies. Firearms and related goods fall under Schedule 6, and weapons under Schedule 13, of the Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956. Each item has an import test, for example police certification, official purposes, specified purposes, dealer, or collector.

Since 22 January 2026: handguns need Home Affairs written permission instead of police certification; assisted-opening and straight-pull firearms need a Home Affairs import permit; belt-fed firearms are controlled like fully automatic firearms; magazines over 30 rounds are restricted to official or specified purposes; silencers, speed loaders and skirmish markers (airsoft and gel blasters) have new controls.
Frames and receivers now need serial number marking and physical inspection, and silencers need serial number inspection.
Have photos and technical specifications for each item, including size, material, manufacturer and serial or model number.
Have a scanned identity document (current Australian driver licence, photo ID card, or passport) for an ABF application.
Do not ship until permission is approved. The B710 form says goods must not be imported until permission is approved.

steps.title: Check the item's control and import test
steps.detail: Read Australian Customs Notice 2026/02 and the ABF prohibited goods pages to find whether your item falls under Schedule 6 (firearms, parts, accessories, ammunition, imitations) or Schedule 13 (weapons), and which tests you can meet. If unsure, email the ABF.

steps.title: Get state or territory police certification (B709A or B709B) where the police test applies
steps.detail: Apply to your state or territory police firearms and weapons registry. B709A is the firearms police confirmation and certification form; B709B is for weapons such as daggers, blowpipes, nunchakus, crossbows, slingshots, star knives, throwing knives and throwing axes. The signed form tells the ABF you are licensed, or that no licence is needed where you live. Ongoing forms B709DA (firearms) and B709X (weapons) are no longer valid from 22 January 2026; only single-use certifications can be used.
steps.cost: Set by state police (not stated on ABF pages)

form.name: Queensland Police B709 import permit online application

steps.title: Apply to the ABF for written permission where a Home Affairs permit is needed
steps.detail: For Schedule 13 weapons not covered by police certification, complete form B710 'Application for permission to import Schedule 13 Weapons' and choose the category (official purposes, specified purposes, dealer, returned goods, or collectors and museum items). For handguns and other items that now need Home Affairs permission, contact the ABF for the correct application. Attach ID, photos and technical specifications, and evidence for the import test.
steps.timeframe: About four weeks once all information is received
steps.cost: No fee listed on the form

form.name: B710 Application for permission to import Schedule 13 weapons

steps.title: Lodge the application
steps.detail: Email the completed B710 and attachments to FWP@abf.gov.au, or post it to Permits and Strategic Goods Section, Australian Border Force, 3 Molonglo Drive, Canberra ACT 2609. Applications missing required documents will not be processed.

steps.title: Present the original paperwork at import
steps.detail: Present the original police certification form (for example the B709A for imitation firearm parts and accessories) or permission to the ABF when the goods arrive. Firearms frames, receivers and silencers will be physically inspected for serial numbers.

steps.title: Exporting or travelling with firearms
steps.detail: Exporting firearms, parts, accessories and ammunition always needs a Defence export permit. Travellers taking their own firearms overseas may instead need a Restricted Goods Permit through the ABF.

contacts.name: ABF firearms and weapons permits
contacts.note: Handles both enquiries and permit applications. Post: Permits and Strategic Goods Section, Australian Border Force, 3 Molonglo Drive, Canberra ACT 2609.

contacts.name: Queensland Police Weapons Licensing
contacts.note: Other states: ACT police.act.gov.au, NSW police.nsw.gov.au/online_services/firearms, NT pfes.nt.gov.au, SA police.sa.gov.au, VIC police.vic.gov.au/weapons-controls, TAS fas.police.tas.gov.au, WA police.wa.gov.au.

watch_out: Old ongoing police certifications (B709DA for firearms and B709X for weapons) stopped being valid on 22 January 2026. Do not rely on one issued earlier.
Goods that arrived before 22 January 2026 without a valid permit must meet the new rules.
Gel ball blasters and airsoft are treated as firearms (skirmish markers), not toys. Those that look like fully automatic firearms or have attached accessories fall under the strictest item.
Imitation firearms include toys, ornaments and game controllers that look like a firearm, whatever their colour, and need permission.
Parts, accessories and magazines that can be used with a real firearm need written permission.
The Minister can refuse an import permission on public safety grounds.
Do not import until permission is approved; incomplete applications are not processed.

guides.title: Permission to import tobacco, vaping goods and nicotine products
guides.summary: Since 1 July 2019 you need written permission from the Department of Home Affairs to import most tobacco products, including cigarettes, loose-leaf tobacco, shisha and heat-not-burn products. Since 2024 vaping goods need a licence and a permit from the Office of Drug Control, and from 24 July 2026 nicotine pouches must be on the ARTG or exempt. Customs duty on tobacco is charged per stick or per kilogram and is indexed twice a year.
guides.authority: Department of Home Affairs and Australian Border Force (tobacco permits and duty); Office of Drug Control and the Therapeutic Goods Administration (vaping goods and nicotine)
guides.timeframe: Office of Drug Control aims to process a vaping import licence application within 30 working days of a correct and complete application. No processing time is published for tobacco permits.
guides.cost_summary: Tobacco customs duty from 1 September 2026 is A$1.55274 per stick (sticks up to 0.8 g of tobacco) or A$2,587.90 per kilogram of tobacco content, plus applicable taxes. Permit application fees are not published on the pages read.
before_you_start: Tobacco permit needed for: cigarettes; shisha or molasses tobacco; loose-leaf tobacco for pipes or roll-your-own; and heat-not-burn products such as heat sticks and IQOS.

No tobacco permit needed for: cigars; chewing tobacco and snuff for oral use under 1.5 kg; unmanufactured tobacco (controlled separately); and tobacco in unaccompanied personal effects if you are 18 or older, declare it and pay duty and taxes.
You must be 18 or older. Tobacco can only come in by air or sea cargo, not international mail.
Tobacco for sale must meet Australian plain packaging requirements.
Vaping goods (devices, accessories, substances and all liquid nicotine) need both an Office of Drug Control licence and a separate permit for each type of good. Only businesses can get them.

For a vaping licence you need an ABN, GST registration, any relevant state or territory licence, and a National Police Certificate less than 12 months old for the licence holder and each authorised contact.
Nicotine vaping goods also need a state or territory licence to import Schedule 4 substances, and the product must be on the ARTG or notified to the TGA before a permit is granted.

steps.title: Apply for permission to import tobacco
steps.detail: Complete the ABF online 'Application for permission to import tobacco' with supporting documents. Tobacco imports are controlled under regulation 4DA of the Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; heat-not-burn products are also controlled under regulation 5A.

form.name: Application for permission to import tobacco

steps.title: Meet the permit conditions
steps.detail: Permits are not transferable and the ABF may add conditions. Personal-use tobacco must not be sold, distributed, supplied or exported. Breaching conditions can lead to the permit being revoked.

steps.title: Declare the goods and pay duty and GST
steps.detail: Tobacco imports attract excise-equivalent customs duty, indexed in March and September. From 1 September 2026 the rate is A$1.55274 per stick for sticks up to 0.8 g of tobacco, or A$2,587.90 per kilogram of tobacco content for loose tobacco and heavier sticks.

steps.title: Vaping goods: get an Office of Drug Control import licence
steps.detail: Complete the licence application, Schedules 1 and 2 for the applicant and each authorised contact, attach National Police Certificates and state or territory licences, and the checklist. Email it to NCS@health.gov.au. Disposable vape licences are only granted for medical or scientific research.

form.name: Application form: licence to import vaping goods

steps.title: Vaping goods: get a permit for each type of good
steps.detail: Once licensed, apply for a permit for each specific vaping good. Before a permit is granted the product must be on the ARTG or a notice must have been given to the TGA (sponsor notice).

form.name: Application form: permission to import vaping goods

fees.note: From 1 September 2026 (was A$1.52829 from 3 March to 31 August 2026)

fees.note: From 1 September 2026, for loose tobacco and sticks over 0.8 g (was A$2,445.26)

watch_out: Tobacco imported without written permission (where one is needed) is a prohibited import under regulation 4DA of the Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956.
Tobacco cannot be sent by international mail at all; use air or sea cargo.
Since 1 January 2024 disposable vapes cannot be imported without an ODC licence and permit; since 1 March 2024 this applies to all vaping devices, accessories and substances.
Travellers cannot bring nicotine pouches into Australia, and from 24 July 2026 nicotine pouches cannot be imported or supplied unless on the ARTG or under an exemption.
Vaping goods cannot be imported under the TGA Personal Importation Scheme.
A tobacco permit does not exempt you from duty and taxes or from plain packaging rules for tobacco sold in Australia.
Duty rates change every March and September; budget using the rate in force on the day of import.

guides.title: Wildlife trade permit to import or export plants, animals and wildlife products
guides.summary: You need a wildlife trade permit to import or export many animals, plants and products made from them, including CITES-listed species, Australian native species, antiques with ivory or turtle shell, and some pets. Permits are issued under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999, and trading without one can mean up to 10 years in prison and a A$222,000 fine.
guides.authority: National Environmental Protection Agency (per business.gov.au), using the online Wildlife Trade Permits service; guidance pages are still hosted by the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW)
guides.timeframe: Your permit application should be processed within 40 business days (excluding weekends and public holidays).
guides.cost_summary: Application fees apply to some permit types; current amounts were not available on the pages that could be read.
before_you_start: Identify the species and its status: check the CITES Species+ website and the Atlas of Living Australia. Whether you need a permit depends on whether it is CITES-listed, Australian native, or neither. Non-live, non-CITES, non-native items generally do not need a wildlife trade permit.
For CITES specimens, find the CITES appendix (I, II or III), as rules differ.
Work out the purpose: commercial or non-commercial (personal, household pet, research, exhibition and so on).

Commercial imports of CITES-listed specimens need a copy of the CITES export permit from the exporting or re-exporting country when you apply. Appendix II specimens declared for stricter domestic measures must be captive-bred, artificially propagated, or from an approved Commercial Import Program.
Commercial exports of Australian native species must come from an approved commercial source program, be pre-Convention, or be exempt (List of Exempt Native Specimens).
Live export of Australian native mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians is prohibited (limited household pet provisions apply).
Live animal imports also require the species to be on the Live Import List.

steps.title: Check whether you need a permit
steps.detail: Follow the 'Do I need a permit?' steps: species status, CITES appendix, then purpose. Some personal items in your luggage and some household effects can be exempt for certain CITES Appendix II specimens.

steps.title: Register on the online Wildlife Trade Permits service
steps.detail: New applications must be lodged through the online portal. Register an account first.

steps.title: Apply for the right permit or certificate
steps.detail: Options include CITES import and export permits, pre-Convention certificates (for non-live items acquired before the species was listed, which must travel with the item), live import permits, native species export permits, re-export permits, single-use permits (one consignment) and multiple consignment authorities. Attach supporting documents such as the foreign CITES export permit and evidence of legal source.
steps.cost: Fees apply to some permit types

steps.title: Ship and comply with permit conditions
steps.detail: A single-use permit is only valid for one shipment. For re-exports, provide the original CITES export permit and your Australian import permit, and acquit the permit within two weeks of shipment.
steps.timeframe: Re-export permits acquitted within two weeks of shipment

contacts.name: National Environmental Protection Agency (wildlife trade permits contact listed on business.gov.au)
contacts.note: Mailing address: GPO Box 3090, Canberra ACT 2601. business.gov.au suggests talking to the contact officer about eligibility before applying because the rules are complex.

watch_out: Importing or exporting a regulated specimen without a permit can lead to up to 10 years' imprisonment, a A$222,000 fine, or both.

Items can be seized. There are no on-the-spot fines, but you may be charged storage or disposal costs. To get a seized item back you must apply in writing within 30 days and prove it was not involved in an offence.
Antiques containing a CITES-listed or regulated native species, and vintage ivory, need a permit or certificate to move into or out of Australia.
Pets from overseas can need a wildlife permit as well as being on the Live Import List; CITES-listed non-native pet birds need a permit.
A single-use permit covers one consignment only.

guides.title: Biosecurity import conditions and import permits (BICON)
guides.summary: Before you import anything that could carry pests or disease (food, plant or animal products, timber, soil-contaminated goods, used machinery and many others), check the Biosecurity Import Conditions system (BICON). It tells you whether the goods are allowed, what documents and treatments they need, and whether you must hold an import permit before the goods arrive. Goods that need a permit but arrive without one are exported or destroyed.
guides.authority: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF)
guides.publisher: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
guides.timeframe: Permit applications are usually decided within 20 business days for standard (category 1) and 40 business days for non-standard (categories 2 to 5) after payment and a complete application.
guides.cost_summary: Permit application charge A$135 plus an initial assessment fee of A$82 to A$655 depending on category (2026-27), plus A$42 per 15 minutes if assessment runs over. Inspections are charged at A$42 per 15 minutes in-office or A$70 per 15 minutes out-of-office in ordinary hours.
before_you_start: Search BICON for your goods by description, tariff code or scientific name and answer the questions to reach the 'case' that matches your product. The case shows whether the goods are permitted, whether you need a permit, documents, treatment and inspection.
Register a BICON account if you need to apply for a permit or want email alerts when a case changes. You need the account to apply for, track and manage permits.
Check whether you can meet every condition of a standard permit. If you cannot, you must apply for a non-standard permit, which needs a more detailed risk assessment and takes longer.

Line up supplier documents early. Manufacturer's declarations must come from the company that made the goods and are generally issued no more than six months before arrival. Treatment certificates must come from an approved provider.
For sea containers, ask the packer for a packing declaration covering timber or bamboo packaging (ISPM 15 status), any unacceptable packing material and, for FCL containers, container cleanliness.
Use packaging Australia accepts. Solid timber packaging must be treated and bark-free; straw is prohibited; used fruit, vegetable, meat or egg cartons and second-hand sacks are removed and destroyed.

steps.title: Check import conditions in BICON
steps.detail: Open BICON, search for the commodity and answer the questions. Bookmark the case (Bookmark Options) to share it with your supplier or offshore treatment provider; the permanent link can be entered in the 'ICON Link' field when lodging documents in the Cargo Online Lodgement System (COLS). Note every document, treatment and permit requirement listed.

steps.title: Register a BICON account
steps.detail: Create a registered user account in BICON. DAFF offers a 15 minute 'Introduction to BICON' eLearning module and printable task cards in the BICON Help menu.

steps.title: Apply for the import permit in BICON (if the case says one is needed)
steps.detail: Lodge an electronic permit application through BICON. Choose a standard permit only if you can meet all its fixed conditions; otherwise apply for a non-standard permit. Pay the application charge and the initial assessment fee for the category; DAFF will not start assessing until both are paid. The assessing officer will contact you if more information is needed. Paying does not guarantee a permit.
steps.timeframe: Usually 20 business days (standard, category 1) or 40 business days (non-standard, categories 2 to 5), longer if information is missing or the product is novel
steps.cost: A$135 application charge plus A$82 to A$655 assessment fee

steps.title: Get the supporting documents from your supplier
steps.detail: Documents must be complete, legible, in English (or with an accredited translation), unaltered, dated, endorsed by an employee of the issuer and linked to the consignment by a unique identifier such as a container, bill or invoice number. Manufacturer's declarations must be on the manufacturer's letterhead with the signer's name and job title. Treatment certificates must show the provider's letterhead, goods treated, quantity, treatment date and, for fumigation, fumigant, dose, exposure time, minimum temperature and completion date.

steps.title: Prepare the container and packing declaration
steps.detail: Use a clean container. Have the packer issue a packing declaration on letterhead, signed by a named employee, stating any timber or bamboo packaging and whether it is ISPM 15 compliant, treated or untreated, and (for FCL containers) that the container is clean. Annual packing declarations can cover a year of shipments. Timber dunnage needs a valid treatment certificate.

form.name: Packing declaration fact sheet and templates

steps.title: Lodge the documents with your import declaration
steps.detail: Your broker or you lodge the import declaration in ICS and the biosecurity documents through COLS (or the Document Lodgement Service for SAC cargo). DAFF assesses the documents and issues a direction: release, or inspection, treatment, holding pending information or insect identification.
steps.cost: Full import declaration charge A$48 (air) or A$71 (sea)

steps.title: Book and attend any inspection
steps.detail: Book inspections through the Biosecurity Portal (recommended for importers, brokers and freight forwarders, and individuals without an ABN). Inspections happen at the port or airport of first entry or at an approved arrangement site. Some consignments are randomly selected under the Cargo Compliance Verification scheme; no inspection fee applies if those are found compliant.
steps.cost: A$42 per 15 minutes in-office or A$70 per 15 minutes out-of-office in ordinary hours; higher out of hours

steps.title: Deal with non-compliance
steps.detail: Contaminated containers or goods are treated, at your cost. Missing or inadequate packing declarations lead to inspection at an approved arrangement site. Goods that do not meet requirements and cannot be treated are directed for export or disposal at the importer's expense. Goods needing a permit that arrive without one are exported or destroyed.
steps.cost: Treatment, storage and inspection fees at your cost

fees.label: Additional permit assessment time
fees.note: Per 15 minutes or part, beyond the initial assessment period

fees.label: Out-of-office (inspection) fee, ordinary hours
fees.note: Per 15 minutes per person, or A$1,351 daily; out of hours A$88 per 15 minutes continuous

fees.label: Out-of-office fee, weekend or departmental holiday
fees.note: First 30 minutes per person, then A$93 per 15 minutes

fees.label: Full import declaration charge, air / sea
Approved arrangement application charge
fees.note: Only if you apply to run your own approved arrangement site

contacts.name: DAFF Biosecurity Import Support (import conditions and permits)
contacts.note: From outside Australia +61 3 8318 6700; also the Contact Us function inside BICON

watch_out: Do not ship goods that need a permit until the permit is issued. Goods arriving without a required permit, even while the application is pending, are exported or destroyed.
Documents that only link to the consignment by package count, weight or date are not accepted; use container, bill, invoice or lot numbers.
Manufacturer's declarations older than about six months at arrival, or not issued by the actual manufacturer, can be rejected.
Untreated timber packaging or packaging with bark sends the container for treatment, with delays and charges.
If you cannot meet a standard permit's conditions exactly, a standard permit is the wrong permit; apply for a non-standard one.
A varied permit keeps its original expiry date, so apply for a new permit if yours is close to expiring.
If you are unprepared at an inspection it can be cancelled but still charged.

guides.title: Brown marmorated stink bug (BMSB) seasonal measures
guides.summary: During the BMSB risk season, certain goods shipped by sea from target risk countries (the USA, Canada and much of Europe and Central Asia) must be treated for brown marmorated stink bug, either offshore by an approved provider or on arrival. Goods in tariff chapters such as 84 to 89 (machinery, vehicles, vessels) are target high risk. Untreated break bulk, open top and flat rack cargo is turned away and directed for export.
guides.authority: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF)
guides.publisher: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
guides.timeframe: 2026-27 season: goods shipped between 1 September 2026 and 30 April 2027 inclusive. Vessel surveillance runs to 30 June 2027.
guides.cost_summary: No fixed BMSB fee is published. You pay the treatment provider's price (offshore or onshore) plus any DAFF inspection fees (A$42 to A$70 per 15 minutes in ordinary hours) and storage or re-export costs if goods are non-compliant.
before_you_start: Check the shipment date. Measures apply to targeted goods shipped from 1 September to 30 April inclusive (2026-27 season started 1 September 2026).

Check where the goods were made or shipped from. Measures apply to targeted goods manufactured in or shipped from a target risk country. In 2025-26 these were the USA, Canada and most of Europe plus Russia, Turkey, Ukraine, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Confirm the 2026-27 list on the DAFF BMSB page.

Japan, China and the Republic of Korea were heightened vessel surveillance countries (not mandatory cargo treatment) in 2025-26; the UK, China, Japan and Korea were emerging risk countries with random inspection of target goods. Goods made in a target risk country but shipped via another country are still caught.

Check the tariff chapter. Target high risk goods (mandatory treatment): chapters 44, 45, 57, 68, 69, 70, 72 to 76, 78 to 89. Target risk goods (random inspection): chapters 27, 28, 29, 38, 39, 40, 48, 49, 56.
Check the shipping mode. Break bulk, open top, flat rack and modified containers must be treated offshore. Sealed, six hard-sided containers can be treated offshore or on arrival.
For the 2026-27 season the Safeguarding Arrangements Scheme and the Rolled Goods Policy have been removed, and ethyl formate has been added as an approved treatment.

steps.title: Confirm whether your goods are caught
steps.detail: Check the shipping date, country of manufacture and shipment, tariff chapter, and container type against the current season's measures on the DAFF BMSB page and in BICON. Goods outside the listed chapters are exempt unless packed in the same container or consignment as target high risk or target risk goods.

steps.title: Choose offshore or onshore treatment
steps.detail: Approved treatments are methyl bromide fumigation, sulfuryl fluoride fumigation, heat treatment and (new for 2026-27) ethyl formate. Offshore treatment in a target risk country must be done by a provider registered under the AusTreat scheme. Onshore treatment is done at approved arrangement sites (classes 12.1 methyl bromide, 12.2 sulfuryl fluoride, 12.3 heat). DAFF recommends offshore treatment, or packing that allows effective onshore treatment, to reduce border delays.

steps.title: Meet post-treatment loading rules
steps.detail: In 2025-26, goods treated in a target risk country before 1 December had to be shipped (break bulk) or the container sealed within 120 hours of treatment finishing. For 2026-27, break bulk goods must meet the relevant post-treatment loading requirements or be retreated offshore before arrival; the rolled goods allowance no longer exists.

steps.title: Lodge the treatment certificate with your declaration
steps.detail: The treatment certificate must meet DAFF's minimum documentary requirements: provider letterhead, AEI registration number for listed providers, goods treated, quantity, date and fumigation details. Consignments treated with ethyl formate onshore by Class 19 accredited persons are reported with the generic AEI 'TREATEDEF' in the Entity Identifier field of the import declaration.

steps.title: Use the new-goods exemption only if every condition is met
steps.detail: In 2025-26, new goods in chapters 82 and 84 to 89 were exempt from mandatory treatment only if manufacture started on or after 1 December of the current season and a manufacturer's declaration stated the start date. Refurbished goods were not eligible. Confirm whether this still applies for 2026-27.

fees.note: Per 15 minutes per person, 2026-27; applies to document and inspection work

fees.label: Diagnostic activity, roll-on roll-off vessel
fees.note: Per vessel, new 2026-27 charge (paid by vessel operators)

DAFF offshore treatments

contacts.name: See. Secure. Report.
contacts.note: Report a suspected stink bug or other pest

watch_out: Untreated break bulk (including flat rack and open top) target high risk goods are directed for export, and can be denied discharge if identified before the vessel arrives.
Treatment by a provider that is not AusTreat-registered, or one under review or suspended, is not accepted.
Mixing target high risk goods with other goods brings the whole container under the measures.
The Safeguarding Arrangements Scheme and Rolled Goods Policy ended for 2026-27; any previous approvals have no effect.
Used vehicles, machinery and parts (chapters 84 to 89) from the USA, Canada or Europe are the classic case needing treatment.
In the 2024-25 season, 104 consignments were directed for export for arriving non-compliant.

guides.title: Register in the Integrated Cargo System to lodge your own import declarations
guides.summary: To lodge import declarations yourself instead of paying a customs broker, you need a Gatekeeper digital certificate from DigiCert, then you register for Cargo Interactive and create a client record in the Integrated Cargo System (ICS). It suits frequent importers; the ABF suggests one-off or infrequent importers use a broker.
guides.authority: Australian Border Force (Department of Home Affairs); digital certificates issued by DigiCert under the Gatekeeper framework
guides.timeframe: Not published by the ABF. The certificate step depends on DigiCert approving your account documents and a video ID interview; ICS registration itself is completed online once you have the certificate. Bank account (EFT) registration takes up to 5 working days.
guides.cost_summary: DigiCert Gatekeeper account setup fee A$489.00 including GST, plus the price of each certificate (not confirmed). No ABF fee for ICS registration was found.
before_you_start: Decide whether self-lodging is worth it. The ABF says to weigh how often you import, your staff's skills, the cost of digital certificates and IT, against using a broker. One-off or infrequent traders can use a customs broker and never need ICS access.
You need an ABN to set up an organisation Gatekeeper account. Individuals not acting for an organisation can apply for an individual certificate in their full legal name.

Choose how you will connect: Customs Interactive (the web interface at ccf.customs.gov.au) or EDI through third-party software. EDI software that sends messages needs a Device certificate; bureaus such as Tradegate can host a certificate for you under an MOU with the department.
You need Microsoft Outlook set up to receive encrypted email and Adobe Acrobat Reader DC to sign the user agreement with your certificate.
If you want to pay duty by EFT from your bank account, you will also need form B322 (ICS EFT Client Authorisation).

steps.title: Set up a DigiCert Gatekeeper account
steps.detail: Go to gatekeeper.digicert.com/customs and enter your ABN, then your contact details. Pay the account setup fee by credit card or purchase order. Send the documentary evidence listed in your personalised Account Setup Guide (for example a letter from the Australian Business Register or the Tax Office). DigiCert emails you when the account is approved.
steps.cost: A$489.00 including GST account setup fee

steps.title: Enrol a Certificate Manager and complete the ID check
steps.detail: Nominate a Certificate Manager who approves certificate requests for your organisation. They enter personal details, print the Enrolment Pack (Letter of Authority and Attestation Letter), provide copies of ID documents and attend a video interview with DigiCert. Once approved they get installation instructions; installing needs their mobile phone for an SMS code and, unless already paid, a credit card.

steps.title: Enrol Standard certificates for staff (and a Device certificate if using EDI software)
steps.detail: Each person who will use ICS applies for a Standard certificate with their name, mobile and email; the Manager approves and chooses how to pay. A Device certificate is needed for software that exchanges EDI messages with the department.

steps.title: Register for Cargo Interactive
steps.detail: Go to ccf.customs.gov.au and select 'Register for Cargo Interactive'. Accept the terms, select your certificate, download the interactive PDF agreement, open it in Adobe Acrobat Reader DC, sign it with your Gatekeeper certificate and click 'Submit Agreement'. For an organisation, the person who signs becomes the Signing Authority. The first user gets an activation code by email (to the address in the certificate) and enters it on the Activate Registration page. Later users are 'Pending' until your organisation's Administrator enables them (pending users are kept for 7 days).
steps.timeframe: Same day once you have a certificate

form.name: Cargo Interactive Self-Registration User Guide v2.0 (June 2024)

steps.title: Create your client record in ICS
steps.detail: Log in to Cargo Interactive with your certificate and choose 'Register for ICS Production' (or ICS Test). Click 'Registration', enter the required details and submit. ABN clients have business and postal addresses pulled from the Australian Business Register; non-ABN clients enter details manually and receive a Customs Client Identifier (CCID). Registration is complete once the submission succeeds. If you use third-party software, set up an EDI client site as described in the department's Module 3.2 (Client Maintenance) guide.

steps.title: Register your bank account for EFT payments (optional)
steps.detail: Complete form B322 ICS EFT Client Authorisation to let a brokerage quote your nominated bank account for paying charges, with an optional daily limit. Email a scanned, signed copy to CargoClearanceNSW@abf.gov.au or post it to Cargo Clearance, Department of Home Affairs, GPO Box 9984, Sydney NSW 2001. Check status in ICS under Client Summary View, Bank Accounts.

steps.title: Learn the system before your first live declaration
steps.detail: Use the ICS Test environment and the ABF Industry manuals (for example the import cargo clearance modules) to practise. Watch the ICS announcements, Australian Customs Cargo Advices and Customs Notices for system changes and outages.

fees.label: DigiCert Gatekeeper account setup fee
fees.note: Including GST, as shown on DigiCert's Gatekeeper for Customs guide

contacts.hours: Monday to Friday 7am to 7pm, weekends 9am to 5pm
contacts.note: Cargo Support enquiry form preferred; digital certificate questions use form B323 Digital Certificate Enquiry

contacts.hours: Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm AEST

contacts.note: Listed on the ABF bureaus page as the only bureau with an MOU to host certificates

contacts.name: Department of Home Affairs Global Service Centre
contacts.hours: Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm

watch_out: You are responsible for the accuracy of every declaration you lodge yourself; the ABF will not complete it for you, and false or misleading statements attract infringement notices.
The certificate is tied to a person's legal name or your ABN; keep it renewed or you lose access to ICS.
Older ABF guides mention Symantec, VeriSign or Australia Post ID checks; these are out of date. Current certificates come from DigiCert with a video ID check.
Being registered in ICS does not make you a licensed customs broker and does not let you lodge for other people.
