guides.title: Deferred GST scheme for importers (ATO)
guides.summary: If you are approved for the deferred GST scheme, you do not pay GST on imported goods to the Border Force before release. Instead the deferred amount is reported on your monthly business activity statement (BAS) and, if you are entitled to a full credit, claimed back on the same BAS, which helps cash flow. Customs duty must still be paid at the border.
guides.authority: Australian Taxation Office (ATO), with the Australian Border Force applying the deferral at import
guides.timeframe: No approval timeframe published. If you currently lodge quarterly, the switch to monthly BAS takes effect only from the start of the next quarter, so deferral is not available until then.
guides.cost_summary: No application fee was found. Approval is free; the benefit is not paying GST upfront at the border.
before_you_start: You must have an ABN and be registered for GST.
You must lodge your BAS monthly, lodge online and pay electronically. Quarterly lodgers must change to monthly first.
Your tax returns, BAS lodgments and payments must be up to date (including for GST group members and representatives).

You may be refused if, in the past 3 years, you or a director, public officer, partner or trustee was convicted or penalised by a court for tax, customs, misdescription of goods, fair trading or fraud offences. You must disclose these.

The goods must be entered for home consumption. Deferral covers N10 and N30 declarations and amendments where extra GST is due; it does not cover low value goods cleared on informal (SAC) clearances, TRADEX goods diverted to home consumption, or temporary imports under section 162 or 162A.
Wine equalisation tax and customs duty must still be paid at import even when GST is deferred.

steps.title: Switch to monthly BAS if needed
steps.detail: If you lodge quarterly, change to monthly GST reporting. The change only takes effect from the start of the next quarter.

steps.title: Apply on form NAT 75163
steps.detail: Complete the online form 'Application for approval to defer GST on imported goods' (NAT 75163). It checks your eligibility first; if you are eligible, continue on the same form. Save it to a desktop or laptop with the latest Adobe Acrobat. GST group members need the group representative to also be approved and lodging monthly online.

form.name: NAT 75163 Application for approval to defer GST on imported goods

steps.title: Import as normal; GST is deferred at the border
steps.detail: Once approved, your broker or you lodge the import declaration as usual. Customs duty and other charges are paid before release, but GST is deferred. The ABF tells the ATO each month how much GST you deferred.
steps.cost: Customs duty, Import Processing Charge and biosecurity charges still payable

steps.title: Report and claim on your monthly BAS
steps.detail: The ATO pre-fills the deferred GST amount at label 7A. If you are entitled to a full GST credit for the import, claim the same amount at label 1B on the same BAS, so the two offset. Include the importation in your purchases at G10 (capital) or G11 (non-capital). Example from the ATO: a business with A$2,000 deferred GST shows A$2,000 at 7A and includes A$2,000 in its 1B credits.

steps.title: Reconcile 7A with the ICS GST deferral report
steps.detail: A GST Deferral report is available in ICS (to brokers and importers with a digital certificate) for reconciling against label 7A. If 7A is wrong, first contact your broker or the ABF to amend the declaration in ICS. Contact the ATO through Online Services for Business only if an amendment reduces deferred GST for a previous month, with a copy of the amended declaration or the ICS report.

contacts.name: Australian Taxation Office, Online services for business
contacts.note: Use for deferred GST correction requests

contacts.name: ABF GST reports team
contacts.note: Import history reports are A$66 each

watch_out: Late BAS lodgment or defaulting on a payment plan can get you removed from the scheme. If removed, the ABF holds your goods until GST is paid and you must reapply.
Customs duty is never deferred under this scheme.
Low value goods cleared on a self-assessed clearance are excluded.
Check 7A every month against the ICS report; errors must be fixed on the customs declaration first, not just on the BAS.

sources.title: ATO: What is the deferred GST scheme?
ABF: GST and other taxes
ABF: Deferral of GST
ABF: Accessing ICS information

gaps: The ATO does not publish an approval timeframe for NAT 75163.
The ATO phone number for deferred GST enquiries was not read on an official page today.

The ATO page shows label G11 in its example but does not discuss G10 for capital imports; G10 versus G11 depends on whether the goods are capital purchases (general BAS rules, not confirmed on the page read).

guides.title: Import declaration and customs clearance (Australian Border Force)
guides.summary: Goods you bring into Australia must be cleared from customs control. If a consignment is worth more than A$1,000 you (or a licensed customs broker) must lodge a full import declaration (N10) and pay duty, GST and charges before the goods are released. Consignments of A$1,000 or less that arrive by air or sea are usually cleared on a self-assessed clearance (SAC) declaration, generally with no duty or GST, except alcohol and tobacco.
guides.authority: Australian Border Force (Department of Home Affairs)
guides.timeframe: No fixed lodgement deadline is published for an N10. The cargo reporter reports cargo before arrival, and goods are not released until the declaration is cleared and duty, GST and charges are paid. Allow 30 days if you want a free written Tariff Advice before you buy.
guides.cost_summary: Over A$1,000: an Import Processing Charge of A$50 (electronic, under A$10,000) or A$152 (electronic, A$10,000 or more), plus a DAFF biosecurity full import declaration charge of A$48 (air) or A$71 (sea), plus customs duty at the rate in the tariff, plus 10% GST on the value of the taxable importation. Broker fees, freight, storage and handling are extra and are not set by government.
before_you_start: Work out the value of the whole consignment in Australian dollars. Over A$1,000 means a full import declaration (N10) and payment of duty, GST and the Import Processing Charge. A$1,000 or less arriving by air or sea can usually go on a self-assessed clearance (SAC). International mail uses form B374 instead of a SAC.
Tobacco, tobacco products and alcoholic beverages attract duty and taxes at any value, even under A$1,000.

Check whether the goods are prohibited or restricted and need a permit from another agency (for example biosecurity, therapeutic goods, chemicals, vehicles). If a permit is needed you must use an N10 or a long format SAC, not a cargo report SAC, and give proof of the permission to the ABF.

Decide who lodges. The ABF encourages first-time or infrequent importers to use a licensed customs broker. You can self-lodge electronically only if you are registered in the Integrated Cargo System (ICS) with a Gatekeeper digital certificate, or you can lodge a paper form B650 at an ABF counter (higher charge).

Get the tariff classification right. Classifications and duty rates are in Schedule 3 of the Working Tariff on the ABF website. If you are unsure, apply for a free Tariff Advice (form B102) before you order. It covers one good from one manufacturer and takes about 30 days.

Check whether a free trade agreement (FTA) can lower your duty. Australia has FTAs with, among others, Japan (JAEPA), China (ChAFTA), Korea, the USA, the UK, the UAE, India and ASEAN countries. You must hold valid origin evidence (such as a certificate of origin or an origin declaration in the format the FTA requires) when you make the claim.

Check whether a Tariff Concession Order (TCO) covers your goods. A TCO is a duty concession for goods with no substitutable Australian-made equivalent. Your goods must fall in the tariff classification and precisely match the TCO description.
Have ready: the supplier's commercial invoice, the bill of lading (sea) or air waybill (air), packing list, any permits, origin evidence for FTA claims, and your ABN.

steps.title: Classify the goods and estimate duty and GST
steps.detail: Find the 8-digit tariff classification and statistical code in Schedule 3 of the Working Tariff. Check Schedule 4 for concessional items and the FTA schedules (for example Schedule 11 for Japan, Schedule 12 for China, Schedule 15 for the UK) for the preferential rate. GST is 10% of the value of the taxable importation, which is the customs value plus duty plus international transport and insurance (plus wine tax where it applies). Luxury car tax and wine equalisation tax (29%) can also apply.
steps.timeframe: Same day if the classification is clear

steps.title: Get a binding Tariff Advice if the classification is unclear (optional)
steps.detail: A Tariff Advice is an advance ruling on how specific goods will be classified, for intended imports of new goods. Lodge form B102 'Application for Advance Ruling (Tariff)' (print both sides) or lodge through TAPIN if you or your broker has access, then email the application and supporting documents to tariffclassification@abf.gov.au within 5 days. Give detailed information about the goods; the ABF cannot classify on insufficient information. Once issued you must follow it when importing those goods.
steps.timeframe: Service standard is 30 days; longer in busy periods
steps.cost: Free from the ABF (a broker may charge to prepare it)

steps.title: Arrange origin evidence before shipping if you will claim an FTA rate
steps.detail: Ask the supplier for the origin document the FTA requires before the goods ship. For example, under the Japan agreement (JAEPA) goods must be supported by a certificate of origin from an authorised body or an origin certification document completed by the importer, exporter or producer, valid for one year and for a single consignment. Under ChAFTA a declaration of origin can only replace a certificate of origin if the goods are covered by a current Origin Advance Ruling. Without valid origin evidence the claim can be refused and duty recovered with penalties.
steps.cost: Certificates of origin are issued by authorised bodies, which set their own charges

steps.title: Work out the customs value in Australian dollars
steps.detail: The customs value is usually the transaction value: the price you actually paid or will pay. Include overseas packing costs and any inland freight and insurance you paid before the goods left the place of export; exclude international freight and insurance to Australia. Adjust for commissions and royalties where required. Convert foreign currency at the rate on the day of export published by the ABF. If buyer and seller are related, the transaction value can be used only if the relationship did not affect the price.

steps.title: Lodge the import declaration (N10) or SAC
steps.detail: Electronic: lodge the N10 through the Integrated Cargo System yourself (if registered) or through a licensed customs broker. It must state importer details, goods description, transport details (vessel or flight, bill of lading or air waybill), tariff classification, customs value, origin and any FTA, TCO or permit claim. Paper: lodge form B650 (sea or air cargo) in person at an ABF counter with the bill of lading or air waybill, commercial invoices, proof of identity, and any permits. International mail uses form B374. For A$1,000 or less by air or sea, the cargo reporter can often lodge a cargo report SAC; otherwise lodge a short or long format SAC in ICS.
steps.timeframe: Lodge once the cargo has been reported; goods cannot be released until the declaration is cleared
steps.cost: Import Processing Charge: A$50 or A$152 electronic, A$90 or A$192 documentary (see fees)

form.name: B650 Import declaration (N10) for sea or air cargo

steps.title: Pay duty, GST and charges
steps.detail: Duty, GST, the Import Processing Charge and the biosecurity full import declaration charge are paid before release. Brokers often pay through EFT from the importer's nominated bank account (form B322 ICS EFT Client Authorisation, which takes up to 5 working days to register). If you are approved for the ATO deferred GST scheme, GST is deferred to your monthly BAS but customs duty must still be paid.

steps.title: Answer ABF and biosecurity questions and wait for clearance
steps.detail: The ABF may ask questions about community protection, restrictions, permits or the declaration; answer in writing, through ICS or at an ABF counter. The declaration is also screened for biosecurity, and the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) may ask for documents, order an inspection or direct treatment. Goods are held until all holds are cleared.
steps.timeframe: Varies; biosecurity inspections and treatments add days
steps.cost: DAFF inspection fees apply per 15 minutes if inspected

steps.title: Fix mistakes with an amendment or voluntary disclosure
steps.detail: If you find an error (wrong value, classification, origin claim or TCO), amend the declaration in ICS or give a written error notice to the ABF. A full, truthful and voluntary disclosure protects you from offences under sections 243T and 243U of the Customs Act. It is not voluntary once the ABF has started verification, served an infringement notice or begun proceedings. N10 amendments can also be emailed to postimportsnsw@abf.gov.au. The voluntary disclosure team is at vdi@abf.gov.au and confirms receipt within 5 working days.

steps.title: Keep your records for five years
steps.detail: Keep all documents relevant to the import declaration (invoices, bills of lading or air waybills, contracts, origin evidence, permits, payment records) for five years after the declaration. If you rely on an FTA certificate of origin waiver, keep evidence that the goods meet the rules of origin for at least five years from importation.

watch_out: Infringement notices for false or misleading statements that cause a duty shortfall (Customs Act s243T): individuals pay the greater of 15 penalty units or 25% of the shortfall; companies the greater of 45 penalty units or 75% of the shortfall. Statements without a duty loss (s243U) attract 15 penalty units (individual) or 45 (company).
Notices can be issued up to one year after detection or four years after the offence. You usually have 28 days to pay. Unpaid notices can lead to prosecution and the court maximum penalty.

An FTA claim is only valid if you hold current, compliant origin evidence at the time of the claim. The ABF has warned that ChAFTA declarations of origin based on expired Origin Advance Rulings are invalid.
A TCO only applies if your goods precisely match its description and tariff classification. Penalties may apply if they do not.
Goods valued at A$1,000 or less cannot be warehoused, and tobacco cannot be warehoused at all.
The A$1,000 threshold applies to the combined value of the consignment (the ABF defines a consignment in Customs Notice 2021/01), not to each item.
Using a self-assessed clearance for goods that need a permit or have biosecurity conditions can lead to penalties, legal action and underpaid duty being recovered.
Fix errors with a voluntary disclosure before the ABF contacts you; once verification starts the disclosure is no longer voluntary.

guides.title: Imported food inspection and food safety requirements
guides.summary: Food you import for sale must be safe and meet the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. Under the Imported Food Inspection Scheme (IFIS), DAFF refers risk food at up to 100% of consignments and surveillance food at 5% for label checks, visual inspection and laboratory testing; food that fails is not released. You are legally responsible for the safety and compliance of the food you import.
guides.authority: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) under the Imported Food Control Act 1992; standards set by Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ)
guides.publisher: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
guides.timeframe: Food is held from arrival until inspection (and test results, if sampled) are back. No official turnaround for laboratory results is published.
guides.cost_summary: DAFF inspection time is charged at A$42 per 15 minutes in-office or A$70 per 15 minutes out-of-office in ordinary hours (2026-27). Laboratory tests are paid directly to the appointed laboratory at its own prices.
before_you_start: Check BICON first. All biosecurity requirements must be met before IFIS food safety requirements apply. Open the food safety case (pink-shaded titles) for your product and note required tests and documents.

Work out whether your food is risk food (listed in the Imported Food Control Order 2019 on FSANZ advice as medium or high risk to public health; DAFF pages name some cheeses and seafood among them) or surveillance food (everything else). Most food from New Zealand is not referred.

Some foods need a recognised food safety management certificate or a foreign government certificate to be imported at all. Ready-to-eat berries and ready-to-eat pomegranate arils (fresh chilled or frozen) need a food safety management certificate (or a recognised government certificate).

Get supplier assurances: food safety system, permitted ingredients and additives, residue, contaminant and microbiological limits (Code Schedules 19, 20, 21, 27), allergen declarations, compliant packaging (Standard 3.2.2), and no unapproved novel foods or irradiation.

Labels must be in English and include the food name, ingredient list, allergens, nutrition panel, importer name and address, lot code, date marking and country of origin information. Labels can be corrected after arrival but before distribution or inspection.
Importing food for sale makes you a food business. Your state or territory food agency may require registration or a licence.
From 21 September 2019 you must keep traceability records: supplier and customer details, food description and batch or lot, transaction dates and quantities.

steps.title: Check BICON conditions and the food safety case
steps.detail: Search BICON by goods description, tariff code or scientific name. Confirm the case matches your product and answer its questions. Note any import permit, certificate, treatment and analytical test requirements.

steps.title: Source compliant food and collect evidence
steps.detail: Ask the supplier for food safety certification, product test results, ingredient documents, specification sheets and sample labels. For foods that need a food safety management certificate, the certificate must be from an accredited certification body, cover one producer, be based on HACCP principles, be verifiable online, and be current at the time of import.

steps.title: Lodge the full import declaration with food details
steps.detail: Your broker or you lodge a full import declaration in ICS for every food shipment. For certified foods, choose document type 'FSMC' and enter the certificate number. Some cheeses and seafood also need a separate IFIS Importer Declaration lodged in COLS. ICS profiles refer the shipment to DAFF.
steps.cost: A$48 (air) or A$71 (sea) biosecurity declaration charge plus ABF charges

steps.title: Read the Food Control Certificate
steps.detail: If referred, you receive a Food Control Certificate (FCC) listing which lines are inspected, which tests apply and any holding orders. The food must stay on hold and cannot be distributed.

steps.title: Nominate a laboratory if tests apply
steps.detail: Choose an appointed IFIS analyst that can do the tests, confirm it services your location, and complete the laboratory nomination form (single consignment or ongoing). You cannot book the inspection until the laboratory accepts. You pay the laboratory directly.

steps.title: Book the inspection
steps.detail: Book through the Biosecurity Portal or the Request for Inspection form. Eligible label and visual surveillance inspections can be done virtually in Microsoft Teams after registering via importedfood-postinspection@aff.gov.au; food under a holding order, food being tested and supplementary sports foods must be inspected in person. Have the food visible and accessible and documents ready.
steps.cost: A$42 per 15 minutes in-office, A$70 per 15 minutes out-of-office (ordinary hours)

steps.title: Get the result and act on it
steps.detail: An electronic Imported Food Inspection Report is issued at inspection, and an Imported Food Inspection Advice (IFIA) confirms the outcome (after test results if sampled). If the food fails it cannot be released: relabel it (for label failures) or destroy or re-export it under supervision. A failure puts future consignments to 100% inspection until 5 consecutive passes.
steps.timeframe: Label-only results at or shortly after inspection; tested food after lab results
steps.cost: Re-inspection fees, relabelling, destruction or re-export at your cost

steps.title: Consider a Food Import Compliance Agreement as you grow
steps.detail: Importers with a documented food safety management system can enter a Food Import Compliance Agreement (FICA). Food covered by a FICA is not referred to IFIS; DAFF audits the system instead.
steps.cost: A$215 application charge; A$2,966 (single) or A$3,442 (multiple) annual charge

watch_out: You are legally responsible for the food you import being safe and meeting the Food Standards Code, even if the supplier said it complied.
Food on hold must not be moved or sold before release; it must be available for inspection.
A surveillance food that fails triggers a holding order: every future consignment of that food is inspected at 100% until five consecutive passes.
Risk food starts at 100% inspection, drops to 25% after 5 passes and 5% after a further 20, and returns to 100% on any failure.
Missing English labels, allergen statements or country of origin labels are common failure reasons; fix labels before inspection.
Foods requiring a food safety management or government certificate cannot be imported without a valid one.
If you are not ready at inspection, it can be cancelled and still charged.

guides.title: Vehicle import approval (Road Vehicle Standards Act)
guides.summary: Before a used car leaves Japan you must hold an approval under the Road Vehicle Standards Act 2018, applied for in the federal ROVER portal. For a private Japanese import this is almost always a concessional RAV entry approval (older vehicle, SEVs vehicle modified by a workshop, or personal effects), which also counts as your import approval. Without it the ABF will not release the car and you can face penalties, storage costs, export or destruction.
guides.authority: Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts (Road Vehicle Standards)
guides.publisher: Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
guides.timeframe: Allow a couple of weeks to verify your identity in ROVER, then up to 30 business days for the decision (a legislated limit; the clock stops while you answer any request for more information). Apply well before you book shipping.
guides.cost_summary: Older vehicle (25+ years) A$42.20 for a passenger car; SEVs car to be modified by a workshop A$95 application plus a A$109 RAV entry charge; personal effects A$57.20. Fees include or add the per-vehicle RAV charge as noted.
before_you_start: Work out which pathway fits your car. Older vehicles: the car (passenger car, van or light commercial under 3,500 kg GVM) must have been built, or significantly modified, more than 25 years before you apply. If the build month cannot be shown, December of the build year is assumed.

SEVs pathway (cars under 25 years old): the exact model and build date range must have a current entry on the Specialist and Enthusiast Vehicles (SEVs) Register when you apply AND when the decision is made, and there must be an approved Model Report covering your variant held by a Registered Automotive Workshop (RAW) you can use.

Personal effects pathway: only for migrants or Australians returning permanently who personally owned AND used the car overseas for at least 12 continuous months immediately before arriving. You must apply within 6 months of first arriving, and you cannot have had a personal effects approval in the last 5 years. A company cannot use this pathway.

Check the SEVs Register in ROVER (rover.infrastructure.gov.au, public search) for your exact model, model code and build date range. Entries expire after 3 years and cannot be renewed, so check the expiry date. If your model is not listed, anyone can apply to add it (A$230), but a listing does not guarantee your car can be complied.

Have the build date evidence ready. The guide accepts an original sales document, a deregistration certificate from certain countries (for Japan, the export or deregistration certificate is commonly used), or a photo of the VIN, chassis number or plate. The build date of a modified car is the original car's build date.

Create a ROVER account and verify your identity (100 points of ID). The department says verification can take a couple of weeks, so do this first. An agent can apply for you only with an authority to act set up in ROVER.

Ask Queensland TMR (13 23 80) whether the car can be registered before you buy. An approval does not guarantee state registration, and in Queensland light vehicles under 25 years old must be right-hand drive.
Do not book shipping until the approval is granted. The ABF says it is an offence to import a road vehicle without an approval, regardless of value.

steps.title: Confirm the car is a road vehicle and pick the pathway
steps.detail: Use the department's 8 steps guide. For a used Japanese car the usual pathways are concessional RAV entry approvals: Older vehicles (built more than 25 years before you apply), Vehicles to be modified by a RAW (SEVs Register cars), or Personal effects. A Japanese-market car is not covered by an Australian type approval just because the same model name was sold here; if you think it is identical to a type-approved vehicle, the guide says to apply under Personal effects and note 'Otherwise suitable for entry on the RAV' in the comments, ideally with information from the type approval holder. Race, display or film cars that will not be driven on public roads use a non-RAV entry import approval (A$60) and cannot get general registration.

steps.title: Check the SEVs Register and Model Report (cars under 25 years old)
steps.detail: Search the SEVs Register in ROVER for the make, model, model code and build date range. Your car's build date must fall inside the range, and the entry must stay current until the decision. Then find a RAW whose approved Model Report covers your variant (ROVER public search lists RAWs and their scope). The RAW will also need to check damage and corrosion limits, so share auction sheet photos before you bid.

steps.title: Create and verify your ROVER account
steps.detail: Register at rover.infrastructure.gov.au and complete identity verification (100 points of ID). If a broker or compliance workshop will apply for you, set up their authority to act in ROVER.
steps.timeframe: Up to a couple of weeks

steps.title: Buy, or sign a contract to buy, the car
steps.detail: For the RAW pathway you must show you own or intend to own the car (purchase or deposit receipt, or a contract of sale). Older vehicle and personal effects applications also need ownership and build date evidence. Keep the Japanese export or deregistration certificate, auction sheet and invoice.

steps.title: Lodge a Single Road Vehicle Approval application
steps.detail: In ROVER choose New Applications, Single Road Vehicle Approval, answer the vehicle use questions, then enter make, model, year of manufacture, VIN or chassis number and country of import. Upload photos of the front, rear, both sides, VIN and compliance or manufacturer's plate, odometer and engine. RAW pathway: also give the SEVs entry number, Model Report number and its approval holder. Older vehicles: build date evidence and details and dates of any significant modifications. Personal effects: 12 months of ownership and use evidence, arrival date, intent to stay and entitlement to live here (do not upload a tax file number).

form.name: Single Road Vehicle Approval (ROVER online form)

steps.title: Pay the fee so assessment can start
steps.detail: ROVER asks for payment by Visa or Mastercard when you submit. The application is not assessed until it is paid, and it can be refused for consideration if not paid within 30 business days.

steps.title: Answer any request for information
steps.detail: If the department asks for more information or an inspection, you have 30 business days (or longer if stated) to respond. The status shows 'On hold - query pending' and the 30 business day decision clock pauses.
steps.timeframe: Up to 30 business days to respond

steps.title: Receive the approval and read its conditions
steps.detail: The approval is emailed with a unique approval number. It may carry conditions, for example marking a VIN on the car, having a RAW modify it and an AVV verify it, or exporting or destroying it if the RAW or AVV finds structural integrity failures. Breaching a condition is an offence. Older vehicles are entered on the RAV and can take up to 48 hours to appear in the RAV search.
steps.timeframe: Up to 30 business days after a complete, paid application

steps.title: Give the approval to your shipper and customs broker, then ship
steps.detail: Only now arrange shipping. The ABF will not release the car until a valid approval is provided and duty, GST, LCT and other charges are paid. Cars that arrive before approval may incur storage charges or need to be exported or destroyed at your expense.

contacts.note: Phone and email as listed in the ABF asbestos and vehicles factsheet (November 2022). The department's own contact page could not be read by our tools, so confirm before relying on the phone number. Applications are made in ROVER.

contacts.note: Number as listed in the ABF vehicle asbestos factsheet. Valuation questions: valuation@abf.gov.au.

watch_out: Importing a road vehicle without an approval is an offence under section 22 of the Road Vehicle Standards Act 2018: up to 120 penalty units as a criminal offence or as a civil penalty (A$39,600 at the A$330 Commonwealth penalty unit that applied from 7 November 2024; the unit was indexed again on 1 July 2026).
A car that lands before approval can be held in bonded storage at your cost, or have to be exported or destroyed at your expense.
SEVs entries expire after 3 years and cannot be renewed. If the entry expires before your application is decided, the RAW pathway fails.

The 25-year test is about the build date (not the model year or first registration) and is measured at the date you apply. A car whose build month cannot be proven is treated as built in December of that year.

Significant modifications (body, chassis, drivetrain, braking or steering) made less than 25 years ago stop a car qualifying as an 'older vehicle'; it may get a non-RAV style approval but not general registration.
Approval is not registration. Queensland can still refuse registration, and light vehicles under 25 years old must be right-hand drive.

Giving false or misleading information in ROVER, breaching approval conditions or not keeping records are offences that can attract infringement notices, civil penalty orders or enforceable undertakings.
Personal effects: a garaged car, or one with minimal odometer use, does not meet the 'owned and used' test. Only one personal effects approval every 5 years.

guides.title: Asbestos-free assurance for an imported vehicle
guides.summary: Australia bans importing anything containing asbestos, at any level, and the ABF actively targets imported cars and parts. As the owner you must be sure the car contains no asbestos before it ships. If the ABF flags your car you must give evidence; if that is not enough it will direct sampling and testing at the border at your cost, and asbestos parts are seized.
guides.authority: Australian Border Force (Department of Home Affairs), with the Asbestos Safety and Eradication Agency
guides.timeframe: No fixed timeframe. Sort it out in Japan before shipping; a border hold for sampling and testing adds days to weeks of storage and delay.
guides.cost_summary: No government fee. You pay for any parts replacement, technical evidence, sampling by an independent competent person, NATA-accredited testing, and storage while held.
before_you_start: The ban applies to every vehicle regardless of type, age, value or country of origin, and to temporary imports. Japan banning asbestos does not mean a Japanese car is free of it; aftermarket parts are a common source.

List the high-risk parts the ABF names: brake pads and shoes, clutch linings, gaskets (cylinder head, extractors, exhaust), seals (fuel tank, mastic, windows), bonnet liners, heater and air conditioner housings, fibrous washers, sound deadening, firewalls, heat shields, wiring wrap, body seam sealers, bituminous coatings and insulation.

Decide your assurance route before shipping: technical evidence from the manufacturer that OEM parts are asbestos-free, records of replacing at-risk parts with documented asbestos-free parts, or an accredited test report that clearly links to this specific car and the parts tested.
A seller's, supplier's or mechanic's informal statement is not enough evidence. 'Asbestos-free' labels under overseas standards may still allow low levels that are illegal here.
Keep every record (work orders, parts invoices, test reports) and make sure they name the VIN or chassis number. The ABF can ask for them at any time.

steps.title: Assess the car's risk
steps.detail: Consider age, make, model, maintenance history and any aftermarket parts. Older cars and cars with replaced brakes, clutches or gaskets are higher risk. Ask your exporter or the selling dealer for service history.

steps.title: Remove or test suspect parts in Japan
steps.detail: The ABF prefers testing or removing suspect parts before shipment, and notes that replacing them may be cheaper than sampling and testing. Keep work records and evidence of the make, model and composition of replacement parts. Overseas sampling and testing must meet Australian laboratory reporting requirements.

steps.title: Make an honest declaration
steps.detail: Only make a 'no asbestos' declaration if you are certain, covering OEM and aftermarket parts and naturally contaminated materials. Your customs broker will ask about asbestos when lodging the import declaration.

steps.title: Respond if the ABF flags the car
steps.detail: If the ABF considers the car at risk, you (or your broker) must give sufficient assurance with documents. If the evidence is not enough, the ABF directs sampling and testing at the border and supervises it while the car is under customs control.
steps.timeframe: Depends on how fast you supply evidence

steps.title: Arrange sampling and NATA-accredited testing if directed
steps.detail: You must engage a qualified, independent competent person to identify and sample suspect parts; the ABF does not take samples or remove asbestos. Analysis in Australia must be by a NATA-accredited laboratory. Storage costs while waiting are yours whether or not asbestos is found.
steps.cost: You pay sampling, testing and storage

steps.title: Deal with any positive result
steps.detail: Goods found to contain asbestos are seized and forfeited for disposal. Asbestos parts must be removed under ABF control before the car can be released, and you may face penalties.

contacts.name: Australian Border Force
contacts.note: Number as listed in the ABF vehicle asbestos factsheet. Valuation questions: valuation@abf.gov.au.

contacts.name: Asbestos Safety and Eradication Agency
contacts.note: As listed in the ABF vehicle asbestos factsheet (November 2022).

watch_out: Zero tolerance: any level of asbestos is prohibited, including chrysotile (white) asbestos, and 'undisturbed' asbestos is not treated as safe.

Penalties under the Customs Act: section 233 up to 1,000 penalty units or three times the value of the goods, whichever is greater; section 233BAA up to 1,000 penalty units and/or 5 years' imprisonment; companies up to 5,000 penalty units or 15 times the value. The ABF can also issue infringement notices.
All delay, storage, sampling and testing costs fall on you, even if the test comes back clear.
Enthusiast car shows do not count as 'display', so you cannot get a permit to import an asbestos-containing car you plan to drive or show.
Aftermarket brake pads, clutch kits and gaskets bought cheaply overseas are a common cause of detections.
The ABF lists recent detections in imported cars, including a 1971 Mazda RX-2, so older Japanese cars are not exempt.

guides.title: Biosecurity cleaning and inspection for an imported used vehicle
guides.summary: Every used car arriving in Australia gets a full biosecurity inspection inside and out before release. It must arrive free of soil, mud, plant material, insects and animal waste, or it will be cleaned, fumigated, exported or destroyed at your cost. Japan is on the brown marmorated stink bug (BMSB) lists for vessel surveillance and random onshore inspection from 1 September to 30 April.
guides.authority: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF)
guides.publisher: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
guides.timeframe: Inspection is booked after arrival through the local DAFF office at the port; usually days, longer if the car fails and needs cleaning or treatment.
guides.cost_summary: A$71 biosecurity charge on the full import declaration (sea), plus inspection time at A$42 per 15 minutes in-office or A$70 per 15 minutes out-of-office in ordinary hours (2026-27), plus any cleaning or treatment.
before_you_start: You are responsible for the car's cleanliness, inside and out, before it arrives. Risk material includes live insects, soil, mud, animal faeces, leaves, twigs, bark and seeds.
Check the wheels, wheel guards, mud guards, engine bay, underside and chassis rails, boot and spare tyre well, storage compartments, seats and seat folds, vents, and window and door seals.

Consider using a recognised offshore cleaning and pre-inspection provider (ROCIP) in Japan. Fully approved facilities get a 5% onshore verification rate instead of a full inspection. In September 2025 DAFF listed 17 approved facilities in Japan (JEVIC, Autoterminal Japan, Automotive Technologies, Bordercheck Japan, FF Forwarding) in Yokohama, Nagoya, Osaka, Kobe, Kisarazu, Kuwana, Yatomi and Kitakyushu.
Remove personal effects, loose items, used tyres or parts packed with dirt; leave the keys with the car so officers can open all compartments.
Check BICON (the Biosecurity Import Conditions system) for your goods if you are also shipping parts, tyres or other items in the container.

steps.title: Clean the car thoroughly before export
steps.detail: Steam clean the underside, wheel arches and engine bay and vacuum the interior, or book a ROCIP-approved facility in Japan to clean and pre-inspect it and issue certification. The department's 8 steps guide says to steam clean the vehicle inside and out before shipping.

steps.title: Check BMSB season rules for your shipping date
steps.detail: BMSB measures apply to targeted goods shipped from target risk countries between 1 September and 30 April (shipped-on-board date). Vehicles (tariff chapter 87) are target high risk goods needing mandatory treatment when shipped from target risk countries. Japan is listed as a target risk country for heightened vessel surveillance only, and as an emerging risk country, so goods shipped from Japan in that period may be selected for random onshore inspection. Ro-Ro ships that call at target risk countries also face a mandatory seasonal pest inspection on arrival.

steps.title: Make sure biosecurity is covered in the import declaration
steps.detail: Your customs broker's full import declaration is referred for biosecurity assessment and attracts the sea cargo biosecurity charge. The 8 steps guide describes this as lodging a quarantine entry and booking an inspection.

steps.title: Book the inspection with the local DAFF office
steps.detail: Contact the department's office at the port of arrival (Brisbane for most Queensland imports) for the inspection process and documents. Used vehicles get a full external and internal inspection. You or your broker may need to attend.
steps.timeframe: Usually within days of the car being available

steps.title: Fix any contamination
steps.detail: If risk material is found, the car must be cleaned or treated (for example fumigated) at an approved place, re-inspected, or exported or destroyed, all at your expense.
steps.cost: Cleaning and re-inspection at your cost

steps.title: Receive biosecurity release
steps.detail: Once cleared, the biosecurity direction is lifted so the ABF can release the car (if duty and taxes are also paid).

fees.label: Biosecurity charge on a full import declaration (sea)
fees.note: From 1 July 2026, collected by the ABF on goods valued over A$1,000.

fees.label: Inspection or assessment, in-office, ordinary hours
Inspection, out-of-office, ordinary hours
fees.note: Per 15 minutes per officer (or A$1,351 a day), 2026-27.

fees.label: Out-of-office, weekend or public holiday
fees.note: Minimum 30 minutes, then A$93 per 15 minutes, 2026-27.

contacts.name: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (biosecurity)
contacts.note: General enquiries. To book a vehicle inspection, contact the department's local office at your arrival port (for Queensland, usually Brisbane).

watch_out: A dirty car is cleaned, fumigated, exported or destroyed at the owner's expense.
Japan's BMSB status changed recently: it was added to the emerging risk list on 1 August 2025. Check the BMSB page again for the season you ship in.
If the car is transhipped through, or the ship loads in, a BMSB target risk country (for example the USA or much of Europe), stricter measures may apply.
Ethyl formate became an approved BMSB treatment for 2026-27, onshore and offshore; offshore treatment providers must be registered under AusTreat.
Inspection time is charged in 15-minute blocks per officer, so a heavily contaminated car costs much more to clear.
Hand over the keys. Officers need to open the boot, glovebox and engine bay.

guides.title: Customs clearance, duty, GST and luxury car tax on an imported car
guides.summary: Your car is released only after an import declaration is lodged and duty, GST, any luxury car tax (LCT) and charges are paid. The general duty on passenger cars is 5%, but cars that are Japanese originating goods are duty free under the Japan-Australia Economic Partnership Agreement if you hold valid origin evidence. GST is 10% of the value of the taxable importation, and LCT is 33% of the value above the threshold (A$80,809 in 2026-27).
guides.authority: Australian Border Force; Australian Taxation Office (GST and LCT)
guides.timeframe: Lodge the declaration once the car is in transit; release usually follows quickly once approvals, biosecurity and payment are in place.
guides.cost_summary: Duty 0% (Japanese origin with evidence) or 5%; GST 10% of VoTI; LCT 33% above A$80,809 (A$91,661 fuel-efficient); import processing charge A$152 electronic for values A$10,000 and over; A$71 biosecurity charge; broker fees.
before_you_start: Have your import approval number from ROVER. The ABF will not release the car without it.
Gather the purchase invoice, auction and payment records, Japanese export or deregistration certificate, bill of lading, freight and insurance invoices, and your ID. Keep all documents for 5 years.

Get origin evidence for the JAEPA free rate: a certificate of origin from an authorised body, or an origin certification document completed by the importer, exporter or producer. It must exist when the car is imported and is valid for 12 months from issue. A car built outside Japan (even if sold in Japan) is not Japanese originating.

Expect a valuation question for a used car. The ABF says many used vehicles cannot use the price paid, and the usual method is an expert appraisal of the car's value on landing, which you arrange and pay for.
Decide whether to use a licensed customs broker (the ABF recommends one for first-time or occasional importers) or lodge yourself through the ICS or on paper at an ABF counter.

Check the air-conditioning gas. Cars with HFC-134a (or retrofitted systems holding refrigerant) may need an equipment licence unless the personal use exemption (owned over 12 months, private use) or the low volume exemption (up to 25 kg a year) applies. HFO-1234yf is not regulated. Pre-1996 CFC-12 systems are banned except under the personal use exemption.

steps.title: Engage a licensed customs broker (or get ICS access)
steps.detail: Find a licensed customs broker on the ABF list. Give them your ROVER approval, invoice, bill of lading, export certificate, origin evidence, freight and insurance details and asbestos evidence.

steps.title: Classify and value the car
steps.detail: Passenger cars are in tariff heading 8703, with separate statistical codes for used cars by engine type and size. Customs value is normally the transaction value converted to AUD at the exchange rate on the export date; for used cars that were driven before export or depreciated, an appraisal of landed value (fall-back method) is often required.

steps.title: Lodge the import declaration (N10)
steps.detail: Required for goods worth over A$1,000. Lodge electronically in the Integrated Cargo System, through a broker, or on paper (form B650 for sea cargo) at an ABF counter. Claim JAEPA preference with scheme code JEPA if the car is Japanese originating and you hold valid origin evidence.
steps.timeframe: Once the car is in transit

steps.title: Duty is worked out on the customs value
steps.detail: General rate for most used passenger cars in heading 8703: 5% of customs value. Japanese originating goods: Free under Schedule 11 of the Customs Tariff (JAEPA). Without valid origin evidence the 5% general rate applies; you may later claim a refund if you obtain a valid document.

steps.title: GST is worked out on the value of the taxable importation
steps.detail: VoTI = customs value + duty + international transport and insurance to Australia. GST = 10% of VoTI. GST-registered businesses approved for the ATO deferred GST scheme can defer it to their BAS; duty is still paid before release.

steps.title: LCT is worked out last (if the car is a luxury car)
steps.detail: LCT value = customs value + transport and insurance (if not in customs value) + duty + GST. If it exceeds the threshold, LCT = (LCT value minus threshold) x 10/11 x 33%. 2026-27 thresholds: A$80,809, or A$91,661 for fuel-efficient cars (combined 3.5 L/100 km or less from 1 July 2025). Private importers pay LCT on entry. The ATO's worked example: LCT value A$101,500 gives ($101,500 - $80,809) x 10/11 x 33% = A$6,207.30.

steps.title: Pay the Outstanding Payment Advice
steps.detail: The ABF issues an Outstanding Payment Advice with the processed declaration showing duty, GST, LCT, the import processing charge and the biosecurity charge. All duties and taxes must be paid before release.
steps.timeframe: Same day to a few days

steps.title: Get release once all agencies clear the car
steps.detail: Release needs the valid import approval, biosecurity clearance, asbestos assurance if requested, and payment. Then arrange transport (the car is unregistered; see QLD_VEHICLE_REGISTRATION for moving it).

Import processing charge, electronic, value over A$1,000 and under A$10,000
Import processing charge, documentary (paper), value A$10,000 or more
Import processing charge, documentary, value over A$1,000 and under A$10,000

fees.note: LCT rate 33% on the amount above the threshold (GST-exclusive portion).

fees.label: Luxury car tax threshold 2026-27, fuel-efficient cars
fees.note: Fuel-efficient means 3.5 L/100 km or less combined from 1 July 2025.

contacts.name: Australian Border Force
contacts.note: Number as listed in the ABF vehicle asbestos factsheet. Valuation questions: valuation@abf.gov.au.

watch_out: No valid JAEPA origin document at import means paying 5% duty. A certificate or origin declaration older than 12 months is not valid.
Under-declaring the price, or claiming JAEPA for a car that is not Japanese originating, can bring short-paid duty, offences and administrative penalties.
Many used imports are valued on an appraisal of landed value, not the auction price. Budget for an appraisal if the ABF asks.
We found no official LCT exemption for cars over 25 or 30 years old; age-based claims on broker sites are not in the ATO's list of exemptions.
Inflated or understated freight and insurance change the VoTI and GST; keep the real invoices.
An imported air-conditioning system may need a licence under ozone laws if no exemption applies; breaches are separate offences.
Duty and taxes are payable before release, and storage at the wharf keeps charging while you sort out paperwork.

guides.title: Workshop compliance and entry on the Register of Approved Vehicles
guides.summary: A car imported under the SEVs pathway must go to a Registered Automotive Workshop (RAW), be modified to the approved Model Report so it meets the Australian Design Rules, and be checked by an Authorised Vehicle Verifier (AVV) who enters it on the Register of Approved Vehicles (RAV). Only then can it be registered. The RAV entry replaces the old compliance plate.
guides.authority: Department of Infrastructure (RVS); work done by approved RAWs and AVVs
guides.publisher: Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
guides.timeframe: Workshop time depends on the car and the Model Report; the RAV record appears on the public search within hours of a successful submission.
guides.cost_summary: A$109 RAV entry charge for a passenger car (paid via the AVV), plus the workshop's and AVV's own charges, which are not set by government.
before_you_start: This applies to cars approved as 'Vehicle to be modified by a RAW' (usually SEVs Register cars under 25 years old). Older vehicles (25+ years) and personal effects cars are entered on the RAV through their concessional approval and do not need a RAW.

Choose your RAW before you buy: its Model Report must cover your exact make, model and variant, and its approval scope must cover the type of work. Use the ROVER public search to see each RAW's range of operations.
Choose an AVV whose service type, location and vehicle category scope fit your car. The AVV can be engaged by you, the RAW or the Model Report author.
Ask the RAW for its damage and corrosion limits and send auction sheet photos. A car over the limits cannot be complied and may have to be exported or destroyed under your approval conditions.
Get a written quote and time estimate from the RAW and ask what Queensland registration support it provides.

steps.title: Deliver the car to the RAW after customs and biosecurity release
steps.detail: Arrange transport from the wharf to the RAW. The car is unregistered; in Queensland you can tow it or use an unregistered vehicle permit (see QLD_VEHICLE_REGISTRATION).

steps.title: RAW checks identity, damage and corrosion
steps.detail: The RAW confirms the car matches the Model Report and your concessional approval, and inspects it so the threshold limits of acceptable damage or corrosion are not exceeded. If they are, the RAW must stop and notify the department.

steps.title: RAW modifies the car to the Model Report work instructions
steps.detail: Typical work is set by the Model Report so the car meets the applicable Australian Design Rules. The RAW must follow the work instructions in the required order and stop if any check fails.

steps.title: RAW signs a RAW Declaration
steps.detail: When the work is finished the RAW signs a declaration and presents the car, the declaration and supporting documents to the AVV.

steps.title: AVV verifies and submits the car to the RAV
steps.detail: The AVV verifies the car against the Model Report work instructions and submits it to the RAV. The A$109 RAV charge must be paid before the record appears on the public RAV search.

steps.title: Check the RAV entry by VIN
steps.detail: Search the RAV by VIN. New entries are transferred to the public search hourly. The RAV replaces the compliance plate, but VIN marking (ADR 61/03) still applies. Take a copy of your approval to the Queensland inspection.

fees.label: RAV charge: passenger car modified by a RAW
fees.note: Per vehicle; RVS legislation fees and charges schedule.

fees.label: RAV charge: 2 or 3-wheeled vehicle modified by a RAW

contacts.name: Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts (vehicle imports)
contacts.note: Phone and email as listed in the ABF asbestos and vehicles factsheet (November 2022). The department's own contact page could not be read by our tools, so confirm before relying on the phone number. Applications are made in ROVER.

contacts.name: ROVER public search (RAWs, Model Reports, SEVs Register, RAV)

watch_out: Your approval carries a condition that the RAW modifies and an AVV verifies the car; if the examination finds structural integrity failures you may have to export or destroy it.
A SEVs entry or Model Report does not guarantee your particular car can be complied.
You cannot register the car in Queensland until it is on the RAV.
Do not supply (sell) the car before it is on the RAV; providing a road vehicle to the market for the first time when it is not on the RAV is an offence (120 penalty units).
Anyone with a ROVER account can report incorrect RAV information using RAV Correction.

guides.title: Registering an imported car in Queensland
guides.summary: Once your imported car is on the Register of Approved Vehicles you register it in person at a Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) customer service centre. You need a Queensland safety certificate from an approved inspection station, proof of identity and garage address, and you pay registration, the traffic improvement fee, CTP insurance and vehicle registration duty.
guides.authority: Department of Transport and Main Roads (Queensland)
guides.publisher: Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads
guides.timeframe: Usually done in one visit once the safety certificate is issued; the safety certificate is valid for 2 months or 2,000 km for a private seller.
guides.cost_summary: 12-month registration for a 4-cylinder private car A$864.50 to A$880.50 including CTP (as at 1 October 2026), plus duty of A$3 per A$100 of dutiable value (A$5 above A$100,000), plus a safety certificate inspection up to A$102.70.
before_you_start: Confirm the car is on the RAV (search by VIN) and bring a copy of your import approval. Queensland regulations accept an RAV entry as evidence the car complies; without it TMR can refuse registration.
Light vehicles under 25 years old must be right-hand drive to be registered in Queensland. Ask TMR about any special case on 13 23 80 or vehiclestandards@tmr.qld.gov.au.
Get evidence of identity (for example a Queensland driver licence) and evidence of your Queensland garage address issued within the last 6 months. First-time TMR customers also complete form F3503.
If the car has gas fittings you need a gas inspection certificate under 3 months old; if it is modified beyond its Model Report you may need a modification plate from an approved person.
Check the PPSR for the VIN if you bought the car from an Australian importer, and whether it is recorded as written off.
If you will register it in a business name, bring the business documents and an Authority to Represent (F5225) if someone else lodges for you.

steps.title: Move the car legally to the inspection
steps.detail: You can tow the car on a trailer, or drive it unregistered to the inspection station and then to the customer service centre if you carry a CTP insurance certificate for it. For other trips (for example to a repairer) apply for an unregistered vehicle permit (1 to 7 days) online with a Queensland customer reference number or with form F3523, plus class 22 CTP.

steps.title: Get a Queensland safety certificate
steps.detail: Book an approved inspection station (find one at service.transport.qld.gov.au/findais). It checks tyres, brakes, steering, suspension, body rust or damage, windscreen and lights. The certificate is needed to register an unregistered vehicle. A certificate is not required only if the car has never been registered anywhere (including Japan) and shows 500 km or less, which will not apply to a used import.
steps.timeframe: Same day if the car passes

steps.title: Buy CTP insurance
steps.detail: Choose a licensed CTP insurer. You can buy a CTP certificate before driving to inspections, or pay CTP when you register. Premiums for a private car are A$411.80 to A$427.80 for 12 months depending on insurer.

steps.title: Get a registration quote
steps.detail: Use TMR's online quote to estimate registration, traffic improvement fee and CTP for your car's cylinders and use.

steps.title: Register at a TMR customer service centre
steps.detail: New registrations cannot be done online. Bring the safety certificate, identity and garage address evidence, and import approval and RAV details. At a customer service centre you no longer need to fill in form F3518; at QGAP offices, Magistrates Courts or police stations you do. TMR may require the car to be brought in for inspection, and can issue a replacement identifying number if the original is illegible.

form.name: F3518 Vehicle Registration Application (only at QGAP, courts or police)

steps.title: Pay registration and vehicle registration duty
steps.detail: Duty is charged per A$100 (or part) of dutiable value: hybrid or electric A$2 (A$4 above A$100,000); 1 to 4 cylinders or 2 rotors A$3 (A$5); 5 or 6 cylinders or 3 rotors A$3.50 (A$5.50); 7 or more cylinders A$4 (A$6). A used imported car counts as a used vehicle; for some used vehicles the dutiable value is the higher of what you paid and market value.

steps.title: Fit plates and keep the registration certificate
steps.detail: TMR records the car and makes a registration certificate available to you. Fit the number plates before driving.

fees.note: Plus traffic improvement fee and CTP; as at 1 October 2026.

fees.note: Total with TIF and CTP A$864.50 to A$880.50.

fees.note: Total with TIF and CTP A$1,333.75 to A$1,349.75.

contacts.note: New registrations cannot be done online. Go to a transport and motoring customer service centre (or in rural areas a QGAP office, Magistrates Court or police station that offers registration; call first).

contacts.name: TMR vehicle standards
contacts.note: For left-hand-drive and vehicle standards questions.

watch_out: Driving an unregistered car on a road outside the allowed trips is an offence (up to 80 penalty units under the Queensland registration regulation), and you may have no CTP cover.
A safety certificate can be used for one transfer only and expires after 2 months or 2,000 km for private sellers.
Online 'perpetual registration' schemes are not valid; only TMR can register a car for Queensland roads.
Light vehicles under 25 years old must be right-hand drive; most Japanese-market cars are, but some imports are not.
Registration duty is on the higher of price paid and market value for some used vehicles, so a cheap auction price may not lower the duty.
If the car runs on LPG or has a gas system, you need a gas certificate under 3 months old before registering.
If you change the car's purpose (for example to business use or rental), CTP class and cost can change.

guides.title: Motor dealer licence if you import cars to sell in Queensland
guides.summary: If you import Japanese cars to sell as part of a business, Queensland requires you to hold a motor dealer licence (or work for a licensed dealer). Private individuals selling their own car outside a business do not need one. Under federal law, a car must also be on the Register of Approved Vehicles before it is sold for the first time.
guides.authority: Office of Fair Trading (Queensland)
guides.cost_summary: Individual licence A$1,709 for 1 year or A$3,205 for 3 years; corporate licence A$973 for 1 year or A$1,755 for 3 years; criminal history check A$47.35 per person (from 1 July 2026).
before_you_start: Decide whether this is a business. The Office of Fair Trading says anyone who trades in used motor vehicles as part of a business operation must be licensed; it sets no safe number of cars.

You must be 18 or over, complete the current required training modules from a recognised provider (older AUR99, AUR05 and AUR12 modules are not accepted), and pass suitability checks including a criminal history check.
Every business address must be registered and have a licensed person in charge.
Federal rule: providing a road vehicle to the Australian market for the first time when it is not on the RAV is an offence. Make sure each car is on the RAV before you sell it.

steps.title: Complete the required training
steps.detail: Complete the motor dealer training modules required by the Office of Fair Trading with a recognised provider (CRICOS-registered if you are on a student visa).

steps.title: Gather identity and suitability documents
steps.detail: Certified copies of ID (birth certificate, driver licence, passport or citizenship certificate), proof of qualifications, and for non-citizens a visa allowing work. New Zealand-born applicants need a New Zealand criminal history or no-record letter.

steps.title: Apply and pay
steps.detail: Apply to the Office of Fair Trading and pay the licence fee and criminal history check when you lodge.

fees.label: Criminal history check
fees.note: Per person, unless done by the Office of Fair Trading in the last 6 months.

watch_out: Unlicensed motor dealing is prosecuted in Queensland; courts have imposed fines and imprisonment.
Selling a car that is not yet on the RAV is a federal offence (120 penalty units).
The personal effects import pathway is for your own car only and cannot be used by a company.
LCT and GST rules differ for registered businesses (for example quoting an ABN for trading stock); get advice before importing for resale.

guides.title: Export prescribed agricultural goods: registered establishment, permits and certificates
guides.summary: Prescribed goods such as meat, dairy, fish, eggs, grain, plants and horticulture products can only be exported from Australia if they are prepared and stored at an establishment registered with the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, the exporter is registered, and an export permit (and any certificate the importing country requires) is issued through EXDOC or NEXDOC. Importing country requirements are listed in MICoR.
guides.authority: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF), under the Export Control Act 2020
guides.publisher: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
guides.timeframe: Establishment registration includes a departmental audit; allow time before your first shipment. A plant export permit is typically valid for 28 days from the date the goods passed inspection.
guides.cost_summary: For 2026-27: registration applications cost A$689 (dairy, fish, egg), A$786 (grain, horticulture) or A$854 (meat), then annual registration charges from A$1,180 (horticulture grower or exporter) to over A$15,000 (large dairy), plus per-document fees (for example A$99 for an electronic horticulture phytosanitary certificate) and inspection or audit fees charged per quarter hour.
before_you_start: Classify your goods as prescribed or non-prescribed. Prescribed plant goods in shipments of up to 10 litres (liquids) or 10 kilograms (other) need no export permit, but still need inspection if the importing country requires a phytosanitary certificate.

Check the importing country's requirements in MICoR (Manual of Importing Country Requirements), then confirm them in writing with the importing country's authority (for plants, its National Plant Protection Organisation). Email any differences to the MICoR team before you export.
Contact the department's free export facilitator before applying for registration (recommended for dairy and other commodities).
Find or set up a registered establishment to prepare and store your goods.
Prepare an approved arrangement describing how the establishment meets export rules. The department checks listed staff, any outstanding Commonwealth debt, and audits the establishment.

Set up access to TradeClear, the department's online export, import and biosecurity services portal (the old exports.agriculture.gov.au Export Service address now redirects there). Export permits are created in EXDOC or NEXDOC.
Register your ABN in the ABF Integrated Cargo System and apply for access to the Single Electronic Window if you will get your EDN through NEXDOC.

steps.title: Check MICoR and confirm importing country rules
steps.detail: Look up your commodity and destination in MICoR. Confirm the requirements with the importing country's authority, because MICoR is a guide only.
steps.timeframe: Before you commit to a sale

steps.title: Register the establishment
steps.detail: Apply for establishment registration (freight forwarders, manufacturers, processors, producers and storage facilities handling prescribed goods may need it). The department checks staff and Commonwealth debts and audits the establishment against the approved arrangement.
steps.cost: A$689 to A$854 per application, then annual charges

steps.title: Register as an exporter in EXDOC
steps.detail: Register your exporter details in EXDOC, the department's export documentation system. EDI registration is open to exporters of meat, fish, dairy, eggs, grain, horticulture, skins and hides, wool and meat by-products. You need separate exporter registration if you export your own product.

steps.title: Request an export permit
steps.detail: Lodge a Request for Permit (RFP) in EXDOC (for example plants, grain, meat, fish) or a Request for Export (RFE) in NEXDOC (for example dairy). Gather evidence of eligibility such as a declaration of compliance for each shipment and transfer declarations between registered establishments.

steps.title: Book inspection by an authorised officer (plants and grain)
steps.detail: Your goods must be inspected by a plant export authorised officer (AO) appointed by the department. Book a departmental AO through a 'Request for Plant Exports Inspection Appointment', or use a third-party AO.
steps.cost: Departmental AO inspection A$98 per quarter hour; third-party AO rates are commercial

steps.title: Get the export permit and certificate
steps.detail: After inspection, request RFP authorisation and lodge any post-inspection documents. The department issues the export permit and any phytosanitary or health certificate the importing country requires through EXDOC or NEXDOC.
steps.timeframe: Plant export permits are typically valid 28 days from passing inspection

steps.title: Declare the goods to customs
steps.detail: Get your Export Declaration Number (EDN). For dairy, the department says you can obtain the EDN through NEXDOC once your ABN is registered in ICS.

fees.label: Establishment registration application, dairy, fish or egg
Establishment registration application, grain or horticulture
Horticulture establishment registration, grower or exporter (annual)
Electronic export certificate, dairy
fees.note: 2026-27; meat A$37, fish and egg A$38

fees.label: Inspection by departmental authorised officer (grain or horticulture)
Replacement export document
fees.note: Most commodities, 2026-27 (A$551 for meat and live animals)

contacts.name: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
contacts.note: General export enquiries; an online contact form is also available.

contacts.name: TradeClear support (export registrations and portal)
contacts.hours: Monday to Friday, 9 am to 5 pm AEDT

watch_out: Exporting prescribed goods without an export permit, or from an unregistered establishment, is not allowed under the Export Control Act 2020.
MICoR is a guide only. If the importing country's written requirements differ, tell the MICoR team before you export or your shipment may be rejected.
Plant export permits expire (typically 28 days after inspection) if goods are not exported.
Annual registration charges apply even in years you ship little; part-year rates apply when you register mid-year.
Inspections outside ordinary hours cost extra (for example A$40 for up to 30 minutes on weekends, then A$20 per quarter hour).
Prices from 1 July 2027 are proposed to rise in most categories.

guides.title: Defence export permit for military and dual-use goods, software and technology
guides.summary: If you export, supply or publish goods, software or technology listed on the Defence and Strategic Goods List (DSGL), including commercial 'dual-use' items that could have military or weapons of mass destruction uses, you need a permit from Defence Export Controls before the activity. Firearms, parts and ammunition always need a permit to export. Applications are made through the My Australian Defence Exports (MADE) portal.
guides.authority: Defence Export Controls (DEC), Department of Defence
guides.timeframe: No official processing times are published. Applications go through a completeness check, technical assessment, risk assessment and delegate review; incomplete applications get a request for information, which adds delay.
guides.cost_summary: No permit fee is mentioned on the Defence pages read.
before_you_start: Check whether your item is on the DSGL. Part 1 (Munitions List, ML1 to ML22 plus ML901 to ML910) covers items specially designed or modified for military use. Part 2 (Dual-use List, categories 0 to 9, each split into goods, test equipment, materials, software and technology) covers commercial items that could have military or WMD uses.
Use the self-help DSGL tool in the MADE portal to check control status and get recommended forms.
Even items not on the DSGL can be caught by 'catch-all' controls if there is a suspected military end-use or WMD link. Contact Defence for advice if in doubt.

Intangible supply counts: Defence has separate permit guidance for supplying DSGL technology and software intangibly, supplying it to a foreign person within Australia, certain supplies from outside Australia, and providing DSGL services outside Australia.
You need a Defence Export Controls Client Registration Number (DCRN) before you apply. Registration needs a valid ABN or an ABF Cargo Client ID (CCID), and each contact needs their own email address.
Australian residents log in to MADE through ServiceConnect with a Digital ID such as myID; others use direct login.

Gather end-user and consignee details, a precise technical description of the goods or technology, and shipment quantities. Vague descriptions and missing end-user details are the most common reasons for delays.

For trade with the United States and United Kingdom, check whether you can use the AUKUS licence-free environment instead of a permit (you must be approved and lodge a notification of intent to export).

steps.title: Classify your goods, software or technology
steps.detail: Check the DSGL (2024 edition is current) using the MADE self-help tool. Note the control code. Proposed DSGL changes were under review in 2026.

steps.title: Register for a DCRN in the MADE portal
steps.detail: Log in to the My Australian Defence Exports (MADE) portal and apply for a Defence Export Controls Client Registration Number using your ABN or CCID.

steps.title: Choose the right permit type
steps.detail: Options include permits to export or supply military or dual-use goods or technology (including transhipment and repair or return), permits to supply to a foreign person in Australia, multi-party (project) permits, permits to match contracts, permits for items with in-principle approval, and renewals. Brokering needs broker registration and permits. Choosing the wrong application type is a common error.

steps.title: Lodge the application in MADE
steps.detail: All applications must be completed through MADE. Attach supporting documents (not password protected, no special characters in fields). For permits matched to a contract, give the contract name, expiry date and documentary evidence.

steps.title: Assessment and decision
steps.detail: Applications are vetted for completeness, then Stage 1 classifies the item against the DSGL and Stage 2 assesses the end user and risks against 12 legislative criteria (sanctions, human rights, security, diversion risk and international obligations). A delegate makes the decision. The application may be referred to other agencies.
steps.timeframe: Not published; can exceed a month where US ITAR items are involved (industry testimonial on a Defence page)

steps.title: Export, then keep records and report
steps.detail: Lodge an export declaration with the ABF (goods needing an export permit need one whatever their value). Keep records for 5 years from the date of supply, report transfers where a permit condition requires it, and tell DEC about changes that affect your permits.

contacts.name: Defence Export Controls
contacts.hours: 8.30 am to 4.30 pm AEST

contacts.name: DEC outreach and bulletin subscription
contacts.note: DEC runs monthly webinars and a free eLearning course, 'Navigating Australia's Defence Export Controls Framework'.

watch_out: Supplying DSGL technology or software intangibly, or to a foreign person within Australia, can need a permit even though nothing physical is shipped.
A permit is only issued if the activity would not prejudice Australia's security, defence or international relations.
Failing to keep or produce records when asked may be an offence under the Defence Trade Controls Act.
Common reasons for delays: wrong application type, special characters in fields, password-protected attachments, vague goods descriptions, and missing consignee or end-user details.
If you find you have breached the rules, Defence encourages voluntary disclosure.
Firearms, parts, accessories and ammunition always need a permit to export; Defence will only process firearms exports to Vanuatu with Port Vila Hardware as consignee.

guides.title: Lodge an export declaration and get an Export Declaration Number (EDN)
guides.summary: Before goods leave Australia you must report them to the Australian Border Force on an export declaration if they are worth more than A$2,000, need an export permit (whatever their value), are claiming duty drawback, or are dutiable goods with duty unpaid. An accepted declaration gives you an Export Declaration Number (EDN), your authority from the ABF to deal with the goods for export.
guides.authority: Australian Border Force (ABF), Department of Home Affairs
guides.timeframe: You can lodge up to six months before the export date. If goods are not exported within 30 days of the intended date, withdraw the declaration within the next seven days.
guides.cost_summary: The ABF pages do not list a fee for lodging an export declaration, and there are no customs duties on exports. If you use a customs broker or freight forwarder they charge their own fee (not set by government).
before_you_start: Check whether you need one: goods worth more than A$2,000, goods needing an export permit (any value), goods where you claim duty drawback, and dutiable or excisable goods with duty or excise unpaid.

Check whether an exemption applies: personal effects, pets, goods (including mail) under A$2,000, some temporary imports under section 162A of the Customs Act 1901, diplomatic bags, Australian aircraft and ship spares, Australian Government military goods for the ADF, Australian domestic cargo, and containers for international carriage.

Check whether your goods need an export permit, for example agricultural goods (Department of Agriculture), defence and dual-use goods (Defence Export Controls), wildlife (EPBC permits), or other prohibited exports.
Decide who will lodge. The consignor (exporter, owner of the goods, or an agent for them) lodges. The ABF recommends using a licensed customs broker or agent.

If you lodge yourself, you need access to the Integrated Cargo System (ICS) and your ABN registered with the ABF, or you can lodge a paper form at an ABF counter with proof of identity and a client registration form if required.

Have the details ready: consignee, final destination country, intended export date, mode of transport, port of loading, Australian Harmonized Export Commodity Classification (AHECC) code, goods description and FOB value for each line.
Exports are generally GST-free if conditions are met; check the ATO rules.
Keep all documents for five years after lodging.

steps.title: Confirm a declaration is required
steps.detail: Use the ABF 'Export requirements' page to confirm whether the value, permit, drawback or duty rules require a declaration, or whether an exemption applies.

steps.title: Get any export permit first
steps.detail: If your goods need an export permit, get it before you lodge, because permitted goods need an EDN whatever their value and the permit details go on the declaration.

steps.title: Lodge the export declaration
steps.detail: Lodge electronically through the Integrated Cargo System (ICS), usually through a customs broker. Or lodge an Export Declaration (B957) form, with the B957a supplementary page if needed, at an ABF counter in your state or territory, with original or certified evidence of identity. One declaration covers one consignment (one consignor to one consignee).
steps.timeframe: Up to six months before export

steps.title: Receive your EDN
steps.detail: The ABF outcome is an authority to deal with the goods (your EDN), an authority with conditions, or a refusal. Keep the EDN with your shipping records; you must keep documents for five years.

steps.title: Amend or withdraw if plans change
steps.detail: Lodge amendments as soon as possible, the same way you lodged the declaration. If goods are not exported within 30 days of the intended date, withdraw the declaration within seven days after that 30-day period (electronically or with form B611). Lodge a new declaration if you export later.
steps.timeframe: Withdraw within 7 days after the 30-day window

contacts.name: ABF Cargo Systems Support (ICS help)
contacts.hours: Monday to Friday 7 am to 7 pm, Saturday and Sunday 9 am to 5 pm (NSW time)
contacts.note: The Cargo Support enquiry form is the preferred contact method.

contacts.name: ABF general enquiries
contacts.note: Use the ABF Contact us form linked from the page.

watch_out: Not withdrawing a declaration within the required seven days is an offence.
Goods that need an export permit need an EDN even if they are worth less than A$2,000.
Lodge a separate declaration for each consignment (each consignor-to-consignee shipment).
If any details change, lodge an amendment as soon as possible, the same way you lodged the original.
Keep commercial documents for five years after lodging; the ABF can ask for them.
Some exporters can become 'Confirming Exporters' to declare estimates and confirm later (form B111), but only for certain goods.
