guides.title: Export Market Development Grants (EMDG) from Austrade
guides.summary: The Export Market Development Grants program reimburses part of what small and medium Australian businesses spend on export marketing, as matched funding of A$20,000 up to A$80,000 a year depending on tier. Round 4 (covering 2025-26 and 2026-27) is closed, so the practical step now is to get eligible and prepare for the next round.
guides.authority: Australian Trade and Investment Commission (Austrade)
guides.timeframe: Applications are only accepted when a round is open. Round 4 opened 12 November 2024 and tiers closed when funding ran out (Tier 2 closed the same day). No date for a next round was published on the pages read.
guides.cost_summary: No application fee is mentioned. You must be able to spend at least A$20,000 of your own money a year on eligible activities and match the grant amount with your own funds.
before_you_start: Tier 1 (ready to export, A$20,000 up to A$30,000 a year): turnover more than A$100,000 and less than A$20 million, you have not exported before, and you have completed Austrade-recognised export training and/or the Export Readiness Test. Maximum 2 years of Tier 1.
Tier 2 (expanding in existing markets, A$20,000 up to A$50,000 a year): turnover more than A$500,000 and less than A$20 million, with evidence of recent export sales. Maximum 4 years of Tier 2.

Tier 3 (moving into new key markets, A$20,000 up to A$80,000 a year): turnover more than A$1 million and less than A$20 million, evidence of recent export sales, and a plan to enter one of 27 listed key economies (for example Japan, Singapore, the United States) where you do not already export. Maximum 4 years of Tier 3.

All tiers: a valid ABN you have traded under for at least 2 years, tax compliance, products of substantially Australian origin, and capacity to spend at least A$20,000 a year of your own (non-government) money, excluding the grant.
You can receive EMDG for up to 8 financial years in total (not necessarily consecutive). From Round 4, any year covered by a grant agreement counts, even if you report nil activity.

Eligible activities include keeping an overseas representative, short export promotion trips, consultants for research or promotion, foreign buyer visits, free samples to potential foreign buyers, and intellectual property rights. Tier 1 can include export training.
Get a Government Digital Identity and set up EMDG portal access early; Austrade says to give yourself plenty of time.

steps.title: Check your tier and read the guidelines
steps.detail: Compare your turnover and export history with the Tier 1, 2 and 3 criteria and read the EMDG grant guidelines.

steps.title: Tier 1 only: complete export training or the Export Readiness Test
steps.detail: Before applying for Tier 1 you must complete Austrade-recognised export training and/or the Export Readiness Test and keep the evidence.

steps.title: Prepare your plan to market and evidence
steps.detail: Download the sample application form and write a plan to market using the mandatory template; it must be specific to your business. Gather your ABN and proof of 2 years trading, ANZSIC code, proof of tax compliance (such as a business activity statement), evidence of Australian origin, and evidence of turnover and capacity to spend and match funds.

steps.title: Apply in the EMDG online portal when a round opens
steps.detail: Log in with your Digital Identity and lodge. Applications are assessed in the order received and tiers close when funding is fully allocated, so be ready on opening day. Not all applicants are funded.

steps.title: If funded: submit milestone reports
steps.detail: Your grant agreement sets milestone report due dates and payment schedules. For Round 4, the portal opened on 3 August 2026 for milestone reports covering 2026-27 spending. Required evidence is in Section E of your grant agreement.
steps.timeframe: As set in your grant agreement

contacts.name: Austrade EMDG
contacts.note: Subscribe to the EMDG Update newsletter to hear when the next round opens.

watch_out: Round 4 is closed. Tier 2 closed on its opening day (12 November 2024), so if a new round opens, apply as soon as it does.
EMDG is matched funding: you must fund at least A$20,000 a year yourself and match the grant amount, so plan your cash flow.
Your plan to market must be specific to your business; copied or generic plans are not accepted.
Years under a grant agreement count towards your 8-year lifetime limit even if you claim nothing.
Tier 3 markets must be new to you; markets where you already have sales do not count.
Not all eligible applicants receive funding; applications are assessed in the order received until each tier's funding runs out.

guides.title: Get a bush fire assessment for bush fire prone land (NSW)
guides.summary: If your land is bush fire prone, your application must show the work meets Planning for Bush Fire Protection 2019 (PBP). For a house, extension or granny flat that means a bush fire assessment report or a BAL certificate. Subdividing bush fire prone land also needs a bush fire safety authority from the NSW Rural Fire Service.
guides.authority: Accredited bush fire consultant or your council (BAL certificates); NSW Rural Fire Service (bush fire safety authorities and referrals)
guides.timeframe: A consultant's report usually takes a few weeks. RFS referrals add to the DA assessment time.
guides.cost_summary: Consultant fees are set by the consultant. Integrated development adds $194 to council and $443 to the RFS (2026/27).
before_you_start: Check whether your land is bush fire prone using the NSW RFS bush fire prone land check, or your section 10.7 planning certificate.
Have a site plan showing the building, boundaries and the vegetation around the site.
Know which pathway you are aiming for: complying development (CDC) is only possible up to BAL-29.

steps.title: Confirm the land is bush fire prone
steps.detail: Use the NSW RFS bush fire prone land check or look at your section 10.7 planning certificate. If the land isn't mapped as bush fire prone, you don't need this assessment.

steps.title: Get a BAL assessment or bush fire assessment report
steps.detail: A BAL (bush fire attack level) measures how exposed your building will be to embers, radiant heat and flames. Only councils and accredited bush fire consultants can issue a BAL certificate; the RFS doesn't. For a DA, the report must show the proposal meets PBP 2019. For a single dwelling at BAL-29 or below, council may accept the NSW RFS Single Dwelling Application Kit.

steps.title: Choose your pathway based on the BAL
steps.detail: Up to and including BAL-29, complying development may be possible, with a BAL certificate confirming the site isn't BAL-40 or the flame zone. At BAL-40 or BAL-FZ you must lodge a development application.

steps.title: Lodge it with your application
steps.detail: Upload the report or BAL certificate with your DA or CDC on the NSW Planning Portal. For a DA, council must be satisfied the work meets PBP, or consult the RFS if it doesn't.

steps.title: Subdivision: RFS bush fire safety authority
steps.detail: Residential or rural residential subdivision of bush fire prone land needs a bush fire safety authority from the RFS under section 100B of the Rural Fires Act 1997. This makes the DA integrated development: council refers it to the RFS, and the RFS's terms become conditions of the consent.
steps.cost: Integrated development fees: $194 to council plus $443 to the RFS (2026/27)

steps.title: Build to the BAL
steps.detail: Your builder must construct to the bush fire construction standard for your BAL and any conditions in the approval. Your certifier checks this before the occupation certificate.

fees.label: Integrated development (consent authority)
fees.note: 2026/27, when an RFS bush fire safety authority is needed

fees.label: Integrated development (approval body, e.g. NSW RFS)

contacts.name: NSW RFS Planning and Environment Services
Your local council's duty planner
contacts.note: Most councils offer phone advice or pre-lodgement meetings. Check your council's website.

watch_out: BAL-40 and flame zone sites can't use complying development. Plan for a DA.
Building to a higher BAL can add a lot to construction costs. Get the BAL before you finalise the design.
PBP 2019 is the version in force. A draft PBP 2026 can't be relied on until it is adopted.
Don't ask the RFS for a BAL. Use an accredited consultant or council.

guides.title: Get a BASIX certificate (NSW)
guides.summary: BASIX sets water, energy and thermal comfort standards for homes in NSW. You need a BASIX certificate for every new home (including granny flats), renovations costing more than $50,000, and pools or spas of 40,000 litres or more. You make it yourself in the online BASIX tool.
guides.authority: NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure
guides.publisher: Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (NSW)
guides.timeframe: Same day once your plans and specifications are ready.
guides.cost_summary: $50 for a single dwelling, $25 per dwelling for alterations and additions, plus a $5 Planning Portal fee and a merchant fee.
before_you_start: Have your floor plans, elevations, window sizes and orientation, and the materials for walls, roof and floors.
Know your planned hot water system, lighting, appliances, rainwater tank and landscaping.
Register for a NSW Planning Portal account.
Download the Data Input Checklist from the BASIX pages.

steps.title: Log in to the BASIX tool
steps.detail: Open the NSW BASIX certificate tool from the Planning Portal and log in with your applicant or developer Portal account.

steps.title: Start a project and enter your design
steps.detail: Start a new project and enter the details from the Data Input Checklist. Your designer can do this for you.

steps.title: Reach the targets
steps.detail: Select Calculate to see your water, energy and thermal comfort scores. Change the design or fittings until you pass every target.

steps.title: Pay and print the certificate
steps.detail: Pay the certificate fee, then print the certificate and its list of commitments.
steps.cost: $50 single dwelling; $25 per dwelling for alterations and additions; plus $5 Portal fee

steps.title: Attach it to your applications
steps.detail: Attach the certificate to your DA or CDC, and to the construction certificate application. Show the BASIX commitments on your plans.

steps.title: Build the commitments and get the completion receipt
steps.detail: Your builder must install everything the certificate commits to. Your certifier issues a BASIX completion receipt before the occupation certificate.

fees.amount: $80 for the first two dwellings plus $35 each extra

fees.label: Planning Portal fee
fees.note: Plus a merchant fee for your payment method

contacts.note: Put 'BASIX' in the subject line if you email through the contact page.

contacts.hours: 9am to 5pm, Monday to Friday (not public holidays)
contacts.note: For help using the Portal. Questions about your project go to your council or certifier.

watch_out: If you change the design after the certificate, revise the certificate. Revising a valid certificate already lodged is free.
The certificate must match the plans you lodge, or the certifier will send it back.
Granny flats are new dwellings and need their own BASIX certificate.

guides.title: Get a complying development certificate (CDC) in NSW
guides.summary: A complying development certificate is a fast-track planning and building approval in one. If your house, extension, granny flat or change of use meets every standard in a State code, your council or a registered certifier can approve it in about 20 days (10 days for NSW Housing Pattern Book designs), without a development application.
guides.authority: Your local council or a registered certifier (you choose)
guides.publisher: Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (NSW)
guides.timeframe: About 20 days, or 10 days for NSW Housing Pattern Book development. Neighbours are notified 14 days before approval.
guides.cost_summary: The certifier sets the fee. The Planning Portal charges $43 to submit, plus the NSW BASIX certificate tool fee and any consultant reports.
before_you_start: Order a section 10.7 planning certificate. CDCs aren't allowed on heritage items, in environmentally sensitive areas or at BAL-40 or flame zone bush fire risk, and flood control lots have extra rules.

Find the right code: the Housing Code (houses, extensions), the Low Rise Housing Diversity Code (dual occupancies, terraces), the Housing SEPP (granny flats, lot of 450 m2 or more) or the Codes SEPP change of use provisions.
Have a designer draw plans that meet every standard in that code (setbacks, height, site coverage, landscaping). One miss means a DA instead.
Get a BASIX certificate if it's a new dwelling or work over $50,000.
On bush fire prone land, get a BAL certificate showing BAL-29 or lower.
Have your certificate of title, site plan, design plans, structural plans and building specifications ready.

steps.title: Check that complying development fits
steps.detail: Check the land exclusions on your section 10.7 planning certificate and the standards of the relevant code. Your council can tell you which documents it expects.

steps.title: Choose your certifier
steps.detail: You can ask council or a registered private certifier. Search the Building Certifiers Public Register to check a certifier's registration. Get a written quote: CDC fees are set by the certifier.

steps.detail: The certifier or council tells neighbours within 20 metres at least 14 days before the CDC can be approved. Talking to your neighbours early helps.

steps.title: Get the decision
steps.detail: The certifier checks every standard and issues the CDC, with conditions, or refuses it. If refused, you can change the design or lodge a DA instead.
steps.timeframe: About 20 days (10 days for Pattern Book development)

steps.title: Appoint a principal certifier and give notice
steps.detail: Before work starts, appoint a principal certifier (often the same certifier). They must tell council at least 2 days before work starts. You must also tell neighbours: at least 7 days before in metropolitan areas, or 2 days in rural and regional areas.
steps.timeframe: 7 days (metro) or 2 days (regional) before work starts

steps.title: Build, have inspections, then get the occupation certificate
steps.detail: Your principal certifier inspects the work at set stages. Before anyone moves into a new building, you need an occupation certificate.

fees.amount: Varies: set by the council or certifier

contacts.note: Most councils offer phone advice or pre-lodgement meetings. Check your council's website.

A CDC doesn't need a separate construction certificate, but you still need a principal certifier and an occupation certificate.

guides.title: Lodging a rental bond in New South Wales
guides.summary: Every bond for a NSW residential tenancy is held by NSW Fair Trading (Rental Bonds), not by you or your agent. The bond can be at most 4 weeks' rent. You must offer the tenant Rental Bonds Online first, where they pay NSW Fair Trading directly; if they choose paper, you use the NSW Rental Bond Lodgement form after the agreement is signed. At the end of the tenancy the bond is claimed through the same service.
guides.authority: NSW Fair Trading (Rental Bonds)
guides.timeframe: Registration needs one visit to a Service NSW Centre; an online bond is lodged as soon as the tenant pays.
guides.cost_summary: No lodgement fee was published on the pages read. The bond itself is at most 4 weeks' rent.
before_you_start: Work out the bond: no more than 4 weeks' rent.
Self-managing landlords need a Rental Bonds Online account before the tenancy starts. Agents use their agency's account.
Check the tenant has internet access, a mobile phone, an email address and a BPay, Visa or MasterCard payment method. If not, use the paper form.
You can't require a tenant to use Rental Bonds Online. Doing so can bring a $2,200 fine.

steps.title: Register for Rental Bonds Online
steps.detail: Complete the Rental Bonds Online registration form and take it, with original proof of identity, to any Service NSW Centre (find one on the Service NSW website or call 13 77 88). Once your documents are checked you get emails with your Landlord Code and instructions to activate your account.
steps.timeframe: One visit, then account activation by email

form.name: Rental Bonds Online landlord or owner proof of identity and registration form

steps.title: Invite the tenant to pay the bond online
steps.detail: Before the tenant signs, invite them to lodge the bond through Rental Bonds Online. The tenant creates an account and pays NSW Fair Trading directly by BPay, Visa or MasterCard. You get a notification when it is paid, and NSW Fair Trading sends the tenant a receipt.

steps.title: Finalise the bond
steps.detail: Once the bond is paid and the agreement is signed, log in and complete the 'finalise the bond' task on your homepage. This allocates the bond number.

steps.title: If the tenant chooses paper: use the NSW Rental Bond Lodgement form
steps.detail: Download the NSW Rental Bond Lodgement form from the Links section of your Rental Bonds Online account. Take the bond only after the agreement is signed. Have the tenant sign the form, give them a receipt (or note the payment on the agreement), don't keep the money or bank it in an account in the tenant's name, and lodge the form and bond by post or at a Service NSW Centre.

steps.title: At the end, claim the bond
steps.detail: Submit the claim in Rental Bonds Online, entering any deduction (zero for a full refund). The tenant gets a 14-day notice of claim by email and SMS. If they don't agree, give them the final condition report and any quotes, invoices or receipts within 7 days of claiming; they can dispute by applying to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal. A claim without the tenant's consent can only be made after the tenancy ends. Paper bonds are claimed with the Claim for Refund of Bond Money form by post or email.
steps.timeframe: Refund paid after the 14-day notice period if the tenant doesn't dispute

guides.title: Getting a pool certificate of compliance in New South Wales
guides.summary: A NSW home with a swimming or spa pool needs a pool certificate to be sold or leased. The pool must be on the NSW Swimming Pool Register. Your council or an accredited certifier inspects the pool barrier and issues a certificate of compliance (valid 3 years) or, if it fails, a certificate of non-compliance (valid 1 year). A sale contract can attach either; a lease needs a certificate of compliance (or an occupation certificate for a pool built in the last 3 years). Lots in strata or community schemes of more than two lots are exempt.
guides.authority: Local council or an accredited certifier
guides.timeframe: Book the inspection well before you list or lease; a failed pool needs repairs and a reinspection.

before_you_start: Check whether the pool is already on the NSW Swimming Pool Register and whether you hold a current certificate (compliance certificates last 3 years).
If the pool was built in the last 3 years, its occupation certificate may be enough (with evidence of registration for a sale).
Lots in strata or community schemes with more than two lots don't need the certificate for a sale or lease.
Walk the barrier first: gates should self-close and self-latch, and nothing climbable should be near the fence.

steps.detail: If the pool passes you get a certificate of compliance, valid 3 years. If it fails you get a certificate of non-compliance listing the defects, valid 1 year; fix them and book a reinspection.
steps.timeframe: Report and certificate emailed after the inspection

steps.detail: Your conveyancer attaches the certificate of compliance, an occupation certificate with evidence of registration, or a certificate of non-compliance to the NSW contract for sale of land before marketing. With a non-compliance certificate, the buyer has 90 days after settlement to make the pool compliant.

guides.title: Notifying your food business (NSW)
guides.summary: Every food business in NSW must notify before it starts trading. Cafes, restaurants, takeaways, food trucks, bakeries that sell to the public, school canteens and childcare kitchens notify their local council, which then inspects you. Manufacturers, wholesalers and caterers that don't sell by retail notify the NSW Food Authority, and some of those need a Food Authority licence instead.
guides.authority: Your local council (retail food) or the NSW Food Authority, under the Food Act 2003 (NSW)
guides.timeframe: Notify before you open. Council usually inspects within the first year and then about once a year.
guides.cost_summary: Council notification fees vary (for example A$50 at one regional council in 2024). Council inspections are charged at each council's published rate; the Food Authority charges A$370 an hour (2026-27) for its own inspections and audits.
before_you_start: Work out who you notify. Retail food outlets (cafes, restaurants, takeaways, food trucks, corner stores, retail bakeries), school canteens, children's services and manufacturers or caterers selling direct to consumers notify their council.

Wholesalers, food manufacturers, catering not sold by retail, importers not selling by retail and home businesses selling to other businesses notify the NSW Food Authority, and meat, dairy, seafood, egg and plant products businesses may need a Food Authority licence.
Have your premises fitted out to the Food Standards Code (Standard 3.2.3) before you trade: hand basins, cleanable surfaces, cold and hot holding.
Name your Food Safety Supervisor if you prepare and serve ready-to-eat food; councils ask for their details when you notify.
If you run a food truck or van, check your council's mobile food vending approval as well as the notification.

guides.title: Food Safety Supervisor (NSW)
guides.summary: If your business prepares and serves food that is ready to eat, needs temperature control and isn't sold in its original package, you must have at least one Food Safety Supervisor (FSS) at each premises. The FSS needs a certificate from an approved registered training organisation, valid for 5 years. Since 8 December 2023, food service businesses also need trained food handlers and, for most cafes and restaurants, records of key food safety controls (Standard 3.2.2A).
guides.authority: NSW Food Authority under the Food Act 2003 (NSW); councils enforce for retail businesses
guides.timeframe: Have a certified FSS before you start trading. When a certificate expires, you have 30 days to recertify or appoint another FSS.
guides.cost_summary: The course is paid to the training organisation; prices vary.
before_you_start: Check you're covered: cafes, restaurants, takeaways, pubs and clubs with food, mobile vendors, caterers, supermarkets, delis and bakeries serving ready-to-eat food usually are.
Pick someone who works on site regularly and can supervise food handling. One FSS is needed per premises.
Use a registered training organisation approved by the NSW Food Authority to issue the NSW FSS certificate; a general food safety course alone may not count.
Plan training for every food handler in safe handling, hygiene, cleaning and allergens.

steps.title: Enrol your FSS in an approved course
steps.detail: Book the Food Safety Supervisor course with an approved training organisation. On passing, the RTO issues the NSW FSS certificate.

steps.title: Keep the certificate on the premises

steps.title: Tell council who your FSS is
steps.detail: Give the FSS's name and certificate details when you notify your food business, and update council if the FSS changes.

steps.title: Train all food handlers
steps.detail: Make sure every person handling unpackaged, potentially hazardous food has completed food safety training, and keep the evidence.

steps.title: Keep food safety records (category one)
steps.detail: If you make potentially hazardous food into ready-to-eat food (most cafes and restaurants), record key controls such as receiving, cold storage, cooking and cooling temperatures.

steps.title: Renew before 5 years
steps.detail: FSS certificates expire 5 years after issue. Recertify or appoint another certified FSS within 30 days of expiry.

guides.title: Liquor licence (NSW)
guides.summary: To sell or supply alcohol in NSW you need a liquor licence from Liquor & Gaming NSW. Restaurants and cafes usually need an on-premises licence; small bars (up to 120 patrons), hotels, bottle shops and producers have their own types, and limited licences cover one-off events. You apply online, notify neighbours and others, the application is advertised for up to 30 days, and a complete application is usually decided within 7 working days of that.
guides.authority: Liquor & Gaming NSW; the Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority decides some applications
guides.timeframe: Allow 6 to 8 weeks: up to 30 days of advertising (14 days for a simple restaurant), then usually 7 working days; up to 12 weeks with objections or requests for information.
guides.cost_summary: Application A$965 for on-premises, A$483 small bar, A$965 general bar hotel, A$3,451 full hotel, A$2,760 packaged (from 15 March 2026). Then an annual fee, for example A$811 base for on-premises in 2026.
before_you_start: Check whether you need a licence at all: a BYO restaurant may not, but still has responsibilities.
Use the licence type check on nsw.gov.au to choose the type. On-premises suits restaurants and cafes where alcohol isn't the main business.
Check your development consent allows the use and hours you want; some licence types need consent before you apply.
Get a National Police Check for the applicant and close associates, and ASIC company extracts for a company.
Complete RSA training and, for most new licensees and approved managers, Licensee Training (LT). Higher-risk venues trading after midnight need Advanced Licensee Training.
Some applications need a Statement of Risks and Potential Effects (SoRPE).

steps.title: Lodge online
steps.detail: Submit the complete application through the NSW OneGov liquor portal and pay the fee.

steps.title: Notify stakeholders
steps.detail: After lodging, notify NSW Police, the local council and occupiers of nearby buildings (within 50 or 100 metres, depending on the application) as instructed.

steps.title: Public consultation
steps.detail: The application is advertised on the Liquor & Gaming noticeboard for up to 30 days (14 days for a simple restaurant).

steps.title: Decision and conditions
steps.detail: Complete applications are generally decided within 7 working days of consultation; with objections it can take up to 12 weeks. Display the mandatory signs and keep an incident register if required.

steps.title: Pay the annual fee
steps.detail: Annual licence fees are invoiced each year (due 29 May in 2026). New licences pay a pro-rata fee.

Get public liability insurance; councils usually ask for a certificate noting council's interest.

guides.title: Payroll tax registration (NSW)
guides.summary: Payroll tax applies when your total Australian wages pass the NSW tax-free threshold of A$1.2 million a year. steps.detail: Lodge the annual return after 30 June.

watch_out: Late registration can mean interest and penalty tax.

guides.title: Registering an imported vehicle in NSW
guides.summary: Once your imported vehicle has cleared customs, take it straight to an Authorised Unregistered Vehicle Inspection Station (AUVIS) for a safety and identity check (blue slip). Buy a CTP green slip, then lodge the Transport for NSW Application for Registration at a Service NSW Centre with your import approval, proof of ownership and ID. You pay registration, motor vehicle tax, plates and stamp duty.
guides.authority: Transport for NSW, through Service NSW
guides.timeframe: Usually one AUVIS visit and one Service NSW visit once the vehicle has cleared customs.
guides.cost_summary: Blue slip A$82; registration fee A$84 plus motor vehicle tax by weight (A$391 for a 1,151 to 1,500 kg private car); plates A$32 or more; CTP green slip from an insurer; stamp duty A$3 per A$100 up to A$44,999.
before_you_start: Have your Vehicle Import Approval and, for vehicles that need it, the Register of Approved Vehicles entry.
Light vehicles must be right-hand drive unless 25 years or older (or over 4.5 tonnes GVM).
Bring proof of entitlement (bill of sale or overseas registration certificate) and proof of identity.
Vehicles 5 tonnes or more, with power brakes, trailers over 2 tonnes and big buses go to a heavy vehicle inspection station instead of an AUVIS.

guides.title: Registering a boat in NSW
guides.summary: In NSW a recreational vessel must be registered with Transport for NSW if it has an engine of 4 kW or more, is 5.5 m or longer, is a personal watercraft, or needs a mooring or marina berth. guides.title: Get a planning permit from your council (Victoria)
guides.summary: In Victoria your council's planning scheme decides whether you need a planning permit. The zone and overlays on your land set the rules. If a permit is needed, you apply to the council, which may tell your neighbours and must normally decide within 60 statutory days. You can ask VCAT to review a refusal or conditions.
guides.authority: Your local council (the responsible authority under the Planning and Environment Act 1987)
guides.timeframe: 60 statutory days for a decision once the application is complete, longer if council asks for more information or neighbours object.
guides.cost_summary: Statutory fees for 2026-27: $233.10 to $1,744.30 for a single dwelling depending on cost, $1,537.00 for a use or a 2-lot subdivision.
before_you_start: Download a free VicPlan planning property report to see your zone and overlays.
Order a current copy of title (Victorian title search (LANDATA)) to check covenants, easements and the title plan.
Read your zone and overlay clauses in the Victorian planning schemes online.
Have plans drawn: site plan, floor plans and elevations, and a written report on how you meet the planning scheme.
If you aren't the owner, get the owner's signature or tell them about the application.

steps.title: Check whether you need a permit
steps.detail: Look up your zone and overlays on VicPlan, then read those clauses in your council's planning scheme. Each zone lists uses that need no permit, need a permit or are prohibited, and the buildings and works that need a permit. Overlays like the Heritage, Bushfire Management or Land Subject to Inundation overlays add their own triggers.

steps.title: Talk to council before you lodge
steps.detail: Call the duty planner or book a pre-application meeting. Council can tell you what reports to include, which can save a further information request later. Some councils offer pre-lodgement certification with faster decisions.

steps.title: Prepare and lodge the application
steps.detail: Lodge with your council, usually through its online portal, with the council's planning permit application form, the plans, a current copy of title and the fee. Council can check the application is complete within 5 business days. If it asks for missing information and you don't provide it by the deadline, the application lapses and the fee is refunded.

steps.title: Further information and referral
steps.detail: Council may ask for more information. Some applications are referred to authorities like the CFA, a water corporation or Heritage Victoria, which have 28 days to respond.

steps.title: Notice to neighbours (advertising)
steps.detail: Unless council decides no one would be materially affected, it requires notice of the application: letters to neighbours, a sign on the site, or both, for at least 14 days. Anyone affected can object in writing. Council can't decide until the notice period ends.

steps.title: Council decides
steps.detail: Council issues a permit, a notice of decision to grant a permit (if there were objections), or a refusal. Read the conditions carefully: many must be met before you start, like endorsed plans.
steps.timeframe: 60 statutory days, adjusted for further information requests

steps.title: Ask VCAT for a review if needed
steps.detail: You can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) within 60 days of a refusal or of conditions you disagree with, or if council doesn't decide in time. Objectors can also seek a review of a notice of decision.

steps.title: Act on the permit before it expires
steps.detail: A permit expires if the development doesn't start or finish in the time it sets. You can ask council for an extension of time. Then get your building permit, which must be consistent with the planning permit.

guides.title: Get a 10 day VicSmart planning permit (Victoria)

A single dwelling or small second dwelling on a lot under 300 m2 that meets every deemed-to-comply standard in clause 54 can use it, as can some simple subdivisions and minor works.

guides.timeframe: 10 business days once the application is complete.
guides.cost_summary: $233.10 if the work costs $10,000 or less, $500.80 if more (2026-27).

Have your designer check the plans against every deemed-to-comply standard.
Get a current copy of title.

steps.title: Confirm the proposal is a VicSmart class
steps.detail: VicSmart classes are listed in the planning scheme. For homes on lots under 300 m2, the design must meet each listed clause 54 standard, like street setback, site coverage, private open space and tree canopy.

steps.title: Prepare the plans and information
steps.detail: VicSmart has its own short list of information requirements. Include plans showing how each standard is met and a copy of title.

steps.title: Lodge with your council and pay the fee
steps.detail: Lodge through your council's online portal, marked as a VicSmart application.

steps.title: Council decides in 10 business days
steps.detail: There's no notice to neighbours and no objector appeal. If the proposal doesn't meet the standards, council can treat it as a regular permit application.

steps.title: Review if refused
steps.detail: You can ask VCAT to review a refusal, or apply if council hasn't decided after 10 business days.

contacts.note: Most councils offer a duty planner by phone or a pre-application meeting. Check your council's website.

guides.title: Get a building permit from a registered building surveyor (Victoria)
guides.summary: Almost all building work in Victoria needs a building permit under the Building Act 1993, including every new house, extension and small second dwelling. You choose and appoint a registered building surveyor, either council's municipal building surveyor or a private one. The surveyor checks your plans, issues the permit, inspects the work at key stages and signs it off at the end.
guides.authority: A registered building surveyor (council or private)
guides.timeframe: Usually a few weeks, depending on the surveyor and whether report and consent is needed.
guides.cost_summary: The surveyor's fee, plus the state building permit levy of 0.128% of the cost of work over $10,000.
before_you_start: Get any planning permit first. The building permit must be consistent with it.
Have construction drawings, specifications, a structural engineer's design, a soil report and an energy rating.

steps.title: Appoint a building surveyor
steps.detail: You, not your builder, appoint the surveyor. Check they are registered on the BPC's Find a Practitioner search.

steps.title: Pay the building permit levy

steps.title: Permit issued and work starts
steps.detail: The permit lists the mandatory inspections, like footings, frame and final. Your builder must build to the approved plans.

steps.title: Inspections and completion
steps.detail: The surveyor inspects at each mandatory stage. At the end you get an occupancy permit or a certificate of final inspection.

guides.title: Lodging a rental bond with the RTBA in Victoria
guides.summary: Every bond for a Victorian rental is held by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA), not by you or your agent. The bond is usually at most one month's rent. You register for RTBA online, start the lodgement, and each renter accepts it by email. If you receive the money, you must lodge it within 14 days. The renter can instead pay the RTBA directly or transfer a portable bond.
guides.authority: Residential Tenancies Bond Authority
guides.timeframe: Lodge within 14 days of receiving the bond. Renters have 14 days to accept; lodgement usually completes in one business day.
guides.cost_summary: No lodgement fee was published on the pages read. The bond is usually at most one month's rent.
before_you_start: Work out the bond: no more than one month's rent unless the rent is over $900 a week or VCAT allows more.
Each renter needs their own email address and a mobile number to pass Service Victoria identity checks.
Decide who pays: you (from money the renter gave you), the renter directly, or a portable bond transfer.
If the renter will pay the RTBA directly, they must tell you in writing before you start the lodgement.

steps.title: Register for RTBA online
steps.detail: Create a rental provider account. Add your bank details if the RTBA is to debit the bond from your account.

steps.title: Start the lodgement
steps.detail: Enter the bond amount, property address and each renter's contact details. On the funding page choose 'Rental provider' if you hold the money, or choose renter payment or a portable bond.
steps.timeframe: Within 14 days of receiving the bond

steps.title: Renters accept
steps.detail: Each renter gets an email link to review and accept. If they don't accept within 14 days the lodgement lapses and you can restart it with the same details.

steps.title: Payment and receipt
steps.detail: The RTBA debits your account, or the renter pays by BPAY, direct debit or card (the link lasts 48 hours). The RTBA sends receipts with the bond number to every renter within 7 days; ask if you want one. If nothing arrives within 15 days, call the RTBA.
steps.timeframe: Usually one business day; payments can take up to 8 days

steps.title: Manage and claim
steps.detail: Use your account to accept change requests within 14 days, update details or cancel. At the end of the tenancy, tell the renter in advance if you will claim on the bond (from 13 October 2026), and make the claim through RTBA online. Disputes go to VCAT.

fees.note: Unless rent is over $900 a week or VCAT approves more

contacts.note: Use the online enquiries form; no email address was published on the page read.

watch_out: Lodging late or keeping the bond yourself breaches the Residential Tenancies Act 1997.

guides.title: Registering a pool or spa and lodging a barrier certificate in Victoria
guides.summary: Every pool or spa in Victoria that can hold more than 300mm of water must be registered with the local council. A registered inspector then checks the barrier and issues a certificate of barrier compliance, which you lodge with council within 30 days. The barrier must be re-inspected every 4 years. Rental providers must also keep the barrier in good repair and give the renter a copy of the certificate on request.
guides.authority: Your local council
guides.timeframe: Lodge the certificate within 30 days of receiving it; re-inspect every 4 years.
guides.cost_summary: Council registration and lodgement fees and inspector fees vary and were not published on the pages read.

Find your council's pool registration page through Know Your Council.
Check the barrier, gates and self-closing latches before booking an inspection.

steps.title: Register the pool or spa with council
steps.detail: Follow your council's registration process. Council will tell you when the barrier inspection certificate is due.

steps.title: Fix any issues and get the certificate
steps.detail: Once problems are fixed the inspector issues a certificate of barrier compliance.

steps.title: Lodge the certificate with council
steps.detail: Lodge it with council within 30 days of receiving it. Keep a copy for buyers or renters.

steps.title: Re-inspect every 4 years
steps.detail: Book the next inspection before 4 years pass and lodge each new certificate.

watch_out: For a rental, pool barrier repairs are urgent repairs.

guides.title: Food premises registration with your council (Victoria)
guides.summary: In Victoria every business that sells food must be classified under the Food Act 1984. Class 1, 2, 3 and 3A premises must register with their local council before trading; class 4 premises (for example only pre-packaged low risk food, whole fruit or tea and coffee) only notify council. Most cafes, restaurants and takeaways are class 2. Fixed premises register with the council where they are; food vans and market stalls register once through the state-wide FoodTrader system with their principal council and can then trade anywhere in Victoria.
guides.authority: Your local council's environmental health team, under the Food Act 1984 (Vic)
guides.publisher: Safe Food Victoria, Victorian Department of Health and Victorian councils
guides.timeframe: Example (City of Whittlesea): plans approval within 14 days of complete plans, then progress and final inspections before the certificate of registration. Registration is renewed every calendar year.
guides.cost_summary: Each council sets its own fees. Example, City of Whittlesea: plans approval A$231.75 (classes 1 to 3); registration A$809.20 for class 2, A$1,129.80 for class 1 and A$564.35 for class 3 and 3A when opening January to June (half price July to September). Class 4 notification has no registration fee there.
before_you_start: Work out your class. Class 2 covers any premises handling unpackaged potentially hazardous food (such as meat, dairy, cooked rice or sushi). Class 3 covers unpackaged low risk food or warehousing of packaged food. Class 4 covers only low risk activities. If your activity isn't listed, council's environmental health officer decides.
Sort out planning and building first. Councils check that you have any planning or building permits the premises needs before they register it.
Meat, poultry, seafood and dairy businesses are licensed by Safe Food Victoria (started 1 July 2026), not by council.
Class 1, most class 2 and class 3A premises need a food safety supervisor; class 1 and 2 also need a food safety program. Plan the training before you open.
If you buy an existing food business, ask council about transferring the registration and any outstanding defects before settlement.

steps.title: Talk to your council's environmental health team
steps.detail: Call or email council to confirm your likely class, whether you need planning or building permits, and the council's own forms and fees. Many councils have a business concierge or a food premises design guide.

steps.title: Get your plans approved before you build
steps.detail: Submit a scaled floor plan (often 1:100) with details of benches, sinks, hand basins, finishes, exhaust and equipment. Don't start major work until council returns approved plans and conditions.
steps.timeframe: Example: 14 days from complete plans (City of Whittlesea)

steps.title: Apply to register and pay the fee
steps.detail: Lodge council's Food Act registration application and fee. Council won't assess it until the fee is paid. An environmental health officer confirms your class and whether you need a food safety program and supervisor.

steps.title: Pass the final inspection
steps.detail: Council inspects the fit-out before you open. If it meets the Food Standards Code you get a certificate of registration. You can't trade before then.

steps.title: Food vans, trucks and stalls: use FoodTrader
steps.detail: Create a FoodTrader account, register your temporary or mobile premises with your principal council, and lodge a statement of trade for each event or location. Once registered you can trade anywhere in Victoria. Trading on a footpath or council land also needs that council's permit.

steps.title: Class 4: notify council instead
steps.detail: If council confirms you are class 4, lodge its class 4 notification form. There is no registration, but you still must follow the Food Standards Code.

steps.title: Renew every year
steps.detail: Registration runs by calendar year. Councils send renewal notices late in the year; keep your food safety program audit or assessment and supervisor details current.

You can't trade until you hold the certificate of registration.
Registration doesn't transfer automatically when you buy a business. Apply to transfer it and ask council about outstanding work.
A food van registered in FoodTrader still needs a statement of trade for each location, and a council permit to trade on public land.
Class 2 premises with a food safety program have it audited or assessed every year, which adds cost.

guides.title: Liquor licence (Liquor Control Victoria)
guides.summary: Selling or serving alcohol in Victoria needs a licence or permit from Liquor Control Victoria (LCV). Cafes and restaurants where meals are the main activity usually need a restaurant and cafe licence; bars and venues that don't serve meals need an on-premises licence; bottle shops need a packaged liquor licence. You apply online through Service Victoria, police and council can object, and you display a public notice for 28 days. Decisions take about 9 to 11 weeks.
guides.authority: Liquor Control Victoria, under the Liquor Control Reform Act 1998 (Vic)
guides.timeframe: Apply at least 11 weeks before you need the licence; decisions take about 9 to 11 weeks, longer with objections.
guides.cost_summary: Application: restaurant and cafe A$518.10 to A$1,036.20, on-premises A$690.80 to A$863.20, by capacity. 2026-27 annual renewal base fees: restaurant and cafe A$391.70, on-premises and general A$1,327.50, packaged liquor A$2,655.10, plus risk fees.
before_you_start: Use LCV's liquor licence selector to pick the licence type. A restaurant and cafe licence needs meals to be the main activity at all times.
The applicant must complete, or book, new entrant training and RSA (responsible service of alcohol) training before applying.
Check council needs first: planning permit, food premises registration and any footpath or outdoor dining permit.
You no longer upload a council planning permit; you upload the LCV new licence or permit planning document instead.
Prepare a red line plan showing where alcohol will be sold and consumed, your maximum patron capacity and proof of your right to occupy the venue. Companies need an ASIC extract dated within 90 days.

steps.title: Choose the licence type
steps.detail: Use the liquor licence selector. Restaurant and cafe licences trade 7am to 1am Monday to Saturday and 10am to 1am Sunday; trading after 1am needs a late night licence.

steps.title: Complete the training
steps.detail: Complete or book new entrant training and RSA training. All staff who serve alcohol need a current RSA certificate before you trade.

steps.title: Apply online through Service Victoria
steps.detail: Lodge the application with your documents and pay the fee by Visa or Mastercard. It takes about 45 minutes. Include a venue management plan if you plan live or amplified music.
steps.cost: A$518.10 to A$1,036.20 (restaurant and cafe); A$690.80 to A$863.20 (on-premises)

steps.detail: Display LCV's public notice template for 28 days where passers-by can see it. Police and council are also notified and can object, and the community has 30 days to object. Then email your statement of display to contact@liquor.vic.gov.au.

steps.title: Get the decision and start trading
steps.detail: LCV may ask for more information. When the licence is granted, display it and keep RSA certificates on site.

steps.title: Renew every year
steps.detail: Pay the annual renewal fee, which depends on licence type, trading hours, capacity and compliance history.

guides.title: Footpath trading or outdoor dining permit (Victorian councils)
guides.summary: Putting tables, chairs, A-frame signs or goods on a footpath, road or other council land in Victoria needs a permit from the council under its local law. Each council sets its own rules, fees and renewal dates, and usually asks for public liability insurance and a plan of the area.

Have public liability insurance; ask council for the minimum cover and to be noted on the policy if required.
If you serve alcohol outside, the area must be on your liquor licence red line plan.

guides.title: WorkCover insurance (WorkSafe Victoria)
guides.summary: If you employ workers in Victoria you must register for WorkCover insurance with WorkSafe Victoria. It covers your workers' wages and medical costs if they are injured at work. The only exemption is a business with no apprentices that pays, or expects to pay, less than A$7,500 a year in remuneration.
guides.authority: WorkSafe Victoria, under the Workplace Injury Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 2013 (Vic)
guides.cost_summary: Your premium is based on your industry and the remuneration you pay (wages, super and other benefits).
before_you_start: Remuneration counts wages, salaries, superannuation and other benefits, not just take-home pay.
Any apprentice or trainee means you must register, whatever your wage bill.
Have your ABN, business details, industry and an estimate of the year's remuneration ready.

steps.title: Check whether you must register
steps.detail: Register if you employ anyone in Victoria, unless you have no apprentices and pay under A$7,500 a year in remuneration.

steps.title: Register before your first employee starts
steps.detail: Register online through WorkSafe's website, which directs you to one of its authorised insurance agents. The agent sets up your policy and premium.

steps.title: Keep your remuneration estimate up to date
steps.detail: Each year you declare your actual remuneration so the premium can be adjusted.

watch_out: Not registering when you must can lead to WorkSafe recovering unpaid premiums and penalties (see WorkSafe's premium guideline on failure to register).
Hiring your first apprentice triggers registration even if your total wages are small.

guides.title: Domestic builder registration (Building and Plumbing Commission)
guides.summary: In Victoria, domestic building work worth more than A$10,000 a job, including labour, materials and GST, must be carried out by a builder registered with the Building and Plumbing Commission (BPC, which replaced the Victorian Building Authority). You choose a class: Domestic Builder (Unlimited), possibly with conditions, or a Limited class for particular work such as carpentry or glazing.
guides.authority: Building and Plumbing Commission, under the Building Act 1993 (Vic)
guides.cost_summary: 2026-27 application fees: individual A$1,039.00 (Unlimited) or A$831.20 (Limited); company A$1,454.80 or A$1,163.70. Annual fees from A$415.50.
before_you_start: Check the 'What is domestic building work?' information sheet for the qualifications and experience each class needs.
You need a technical referee report from a domestic builder registered in the same class or a higher one.
Companies and partnerships also register, with a registered builder as director or partner.
From 1 July 2026, builders must also meet Minimum Financial Requirements and arrange Home Warranty for jobs over A$20,000.

steps.title: Choose your class
steps.detail: Decide between Domestic Builder (Unlimited) and a Limited class, based on the work you contract for.

steps.title: Apply through BPC Online
steps.detail: Log in to BPC Online and start a new application from the Registration and licensing page. Upload evidence of qualifications and experience and the technical referee report.

steps.title: Pay the annual fee and keep registration current
steps.detail: Pay the annual fee each year and keep your details and insurance up to date.

watch_out: Work over A$10,000 by an unregistered builder isn't covered by domestic building insurance, and the BPC is running a statewide crackdown on unregistered practitioners.
Queensland's A$3,300 limit doesn't apply in Victoria; the Victorian figure is A$10,000 including GST.

guides.summary: Plumbing and drainage work in Victoria must be done by a plumber registered or licensed with the Building and Plumbing Commission in that class of work. A registered plumber can do the work. A licensed plumber can also supervise apprentices and registered plumbers, issue compliance certificates and do design work, so a plumbing business needs at least one licensed plumber.

Read the Department of Health's infection prevention and control guidelines for your industry.

steps.title: Renew or keep ongoing registration current

guides.title: Provider and service approval for education and care services (Victoria)
guides.summary: Long day care, kindergarten, outside school hours care and family day care in Victoria operate under the Education and Care Services National Law. You need a provider approval and then a service approval. In Victoria the regulatory authority is the Victorian Early Childhood Regulatory Authority (VECRA). Applications go through the national NQA IT System.
guides.authority: Victorian Early Childhood Regulatory Authority (VECRA), under the Education and Care Services National Law
guides.timeframe: Provider approval: a decision within 60 days of a complete application (can be extended with your consent); you are told within 7 days of the decision.
guides.cost_summary: Prescribed national fees, paid online in NQA ITS (see ACECQA's fee information).
before_you_start: Each applicant and person with management or control (PMC) is assessed as fit and proper and needs a Victorian Working with Children Check or VIT registration.
Each PMC completes an online knowledge assessment.
Gather criminal history checks, proof of legal entity, resumes and qualifications.

steps.title: Apply for provider approval in NQA ITS
steps.detail: Lodge the VECRA provider approval forms (PA01 and PA02) with the supporting documents and fee.
steps.timeframe: Decision within 60 days of a complete application

form.name: VECRA provider approval forms (PA01 and PA02)

steps.title: Complete the PMC knowledge assessments
steps.detail: Each person with management or control completes the online assessment.

steps.title: Apply for service approval
steps.detail: Once you hold provider approval, apply for service approval for each service in Victoria.

contacts.name: VECRA
contacts.hours: 9am to 5pm, Monday to Friday
contacts.note: General email vecra@education.vic.gov.au

watch_out: Late payment of the fee can make the application invalid.

guides.title: Registering an imported vehicle in Victoria (VicRoads)
guides.summary: Once an imported vehicle is cleared and on the Register of Approved Vehicles (RAV), you register it with VicRoads. You need a roadworthy certificate from a licensed vehicle tester, the VIN recorded on the RAV and stamped on the vehicle, and for most vehicles built after 1968 a VASS approval certificate and blue modification plate. At the registration appointment you pay the registration fee, the Transport Accident Commission (TAC) charge, a number plate fee and motor vehicle duty.
guides.authority: VicRoads (Department of Transport and Planning)
guides.cost_summary: Registration and TAC charge A$958.80 a year for a car garaged in metropolitan Melbourne, plus motor vehicle duty of A$8.40 per A$200 of market value for most cars (more for luxury cars), an appointment fee and a number plate fee.
before_you_start: You must be at least 16 and the vehicle must be garaged in Victoria.
Vehicles less than 30 years old must be right-hand drive.
The VIN must be recorded on the RAV, for example as 'Concessional - Vehicles modified by a RAW', 'Concessional - Personal Effects' or 'Concessional - Older Vehicles'.
Vehicles built after 1968 (June 1975 for motorcycles) need a VASS approval certificate and a blue modification plate, even if unmodified.
Motor vehicle duty is worked out on the higher of the purchase price and the market value, including GST and Commonwealth taxes such as customs duty and luxury car tax.

steps.title: Get a roadworthy certificate
steps.detail: Take the vehicle to a licensed vehicle tester for a roadworthy certificate. It must be current and original when you register.

steps.title: Get VASS approval and a modification plate if needed
steps.detail: For most imported vehicles built after 1968, get a VASS approval certificate and blue modification plate from a VASS signatory.

steps.title: Complete the registration form
steps.detail: Fill in the VicRoads vehicle registration form. Have evidence of identity and, if someone attends for you, an authority to act as an agent form.

steps.title: Book an appointment and bring the vehicle
steps.detail: Book a registration appointment at a VicRoads Customer Service Centre. Bring your documents, the vehicle (it is usually inspected) and tools to fit the number plates.
steps.cost: Appointment fee, registration and TAC charge, plates and duty

Motor vehicle duty, passenger car up to A$80,567 or low emission
fees.amount: A$8.40 per A$200 of market value or part

fees.label: Motor vehicle duty, A$80,568 to A$100,000
Motor vehicle duty, A$100,001 to A$150,000

watch_out: Online booking isn't available for some vehicles; you may need to call or visit.
Left-hand drive vehicles under 30 years old can't be registered in Victoria.

guides.title: Motor car trader licence if you import cars to sell in Victoria
guides.summary: If you deal in four or more cars a year in Victoria (and sometimes fewer), you need a motor car trader's licence from Consumer Affairs Victoria. You apply through myCAV, need lawful business premises and must show you know the Motor Car Traders Act 1986. Under federal law each car must also be on the Register of Approved Vehicles before it is first sold.
guides.authority: Consumer Affairs Victoria (Business Licensing Authority)
guides.cost_summary: A$2,965.20 combined application fee and first annual licence fee for 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027.
before_you_start: You must be 18 or over and a fit and proper person; the Business Licensing Authority runs a criminal history check and a licensing officer interviews you by phone.
Have premises you can lawfully trade from: a current planning permit or council letter (unless a licensed trader used them in the last 6 months), plus a lease, owner's letter or contract of sale.
Prepare bank statements, a deed of indemnity and a 12-month cash flow projection.

steps.title: Apply through myCAV
steps.detail: Lodge your myCAV motor car trader application with the documents for your business structure (sole trader, partnership or company).

steps.title: Complete the interview
steps.detail: A licensing officer interviews you by phone about the Act and your business.

steps.title: Keep the licence current
steps.detail: Lodge the annual statement and pay the annual fee.

fees.label: Application fee and first annual licence fee
fees.note: 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027; application fee non-refundable

watch_out: Selling a car that isn't yet on the RAV is a federal offence.
Past claims against the Motor Car Traders Guarantee Fund can affect your eligibility.

guides.title: Registering a recreational boat or jet ski in Victoria
guides.summary: In Victoria any boat, jet ski or e-foil that can use an engine for propulsion must be registered with VicRoads before it is used on Victorian waters, whatever the engine's power. Vessels without an engine, recreational tenders and domestic commercial vessels (which AMSA certifies) are exempt. Registration is renewed every 12 months.
guides.authority: VicRoads, for Safe Transport Victoria, under the Marine Safety Act 2010 (Vic)
guides.timeframe: Register before first use; renew every 12 months.
before_you_start: Have evidence of identity and, if you belong to an approved club with a reserved number, the club's approval letter.
To apply by post you need a Victorian driver or marine licence or a VicRoads customer number, and you pay by money order.
Plan where the registration number goes: on each side of the hull, forward of the beam, digits at least 150 mm high (100 mm for personal watercraft, 80 mm for an e-foil) in a contrasting colour.

steps.title: Complete the vessel registration form
steps.detail: Fill in the VicRoads vessel registration form.

steps.title: Lodge it by post or at a Customer Service Centre
steps.detail: Post the form with a money order, or book an appointment at a VicRoads Customer Service Centre.
steps.cost: See VicRoads boat and vessel fees

steps.title: Display the number and label
steps.detail: Display the registration number on both sides of the hull and the registration label where it is clearly visible on the outside or upper part of the vessel.

steps.title: Renew every 12 months
steps.detail: Renew the registration each year.

watch_out: Victoria has no minimum engine power: even a small electric outboard means the boat must be registered.
Commercial vessels aren't registered by VicRoads; follow the AMSA steps instead.

sources.title: VicRoads: Register a boat or jet ski
VicRoads: Boat and vessel fees

guides.title: Victorian marine licence and PWC endorsement
guides.summary: The person driving a registered recreational vessel in Victoria needs a marine licence. You get one by passing an eyesight test and a 30 question knowledge test at a VicRoads Customer Service Centre or an accredited training provider. People aged 12 to 15 can get a restricted marine licence. Riding a personal watercraft (jet ski) also needs a PWC endorsement, which has its own test and a minimum age of 16.
guides.authority: VicRoads, for Safe Transport Victoria, under the Marine Safety Act 2010 (Vic)
before_you_start: Study the Victorian Recreational Boating Safety Handbook (2023 edition) and try the practice tests.
Bring evidence of identity and a completed application form.
If you hold an interstate licence you must convert it if you will operate a vessel in Victoria for more than 3 months.

steps.title: Study and practise
steps.detail: Read the handbook and try the practice marine licence and PWC tests.

steps.title: Sit the tests
steps.detail: At a VicRoads Customer Service Centre or an accredited training provider, pass the eyesight test and the 30 question knowledge test (26 correct). For a PWC endorsement, also pass the 15 question PWC test (13 correct).

steps.title: Pay and get your licence
steps.detail: Pay the licence fee and any PWC endorsement fee.

watch_out: A restricted marine licence holder (12 to 15) can't get a PWC endorsement until 16.
